## [Unreleased]

> **Backfill note (2026-08-04):** Entries below reconstruct the shipped increments between UC-2 (2026-04-24) and the production launch. Each is grounded in merged commits, database migrations, and existing `docs/`. ### Fixed — `main` was undeployable: a credential granted to `e2e-tests` un-skipped 29 specs against a backend CI never starts (2026-09-06)

`2a9482a7` (WIC-2122, pushed direct to `main` with no PR) added `environment: dev` to the **`e2e-tests`** job so the isolation specs would stop self-skipping. They stopped skipping and started **failing**, and the collateral was production delivery: on run `34052242328` `e2e-tests` was cancelled at **15m14s** against its `timeout-minutes: 15`, and because `deploy-production` declares `needs: [lint-and-test, e2e-tests]`, it was **skipped**. `main` shipped nothing from 18:36Z onward (WIC-2201).

**The guard treats "credentials exist" as "a backend is up", and those are different facts.** The specs gate on `test.skip(!process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL, '... require a running backend ...')`. WIC-2122 supplied the credential without supplying a backend, so the guard's premise silently became false. CI has never run the API: `playwright.config.ts` sets `webServer.command` to `npm run dev`, and root `package.json` maps `dev` to the `@wic/web` workspace **only** — the API is `dev:api`, which nothing invokes.

**The blast radius is wider than the isolation specs, which is what made this a deploy-stopper rather than a red check.** The credential gate spans four spec files, and the 29 it woke are precisely `9ed0c01a`'s entire "29 skipped": `multi-user-isolation` 15, `application-form-errors` 7, `auth` 5, `document-storage` 2. The first failure in the run is `application-form-errors.spec.ts:82` — not an isolation spec at all. Each woken spec fails on a ~30s timeout and retries 3×, so the suite cannot finish inside 15 minutes; it reached test 144 of 177 before the runner cancelled it.

**`9ed0c01a` is the positive control, not an argument from absence.** The parent commit is byte-identical config minus this one key and ran **148 passed / 29 skipped in 2.7m**. It also logged **594** `http proxy error … ECONNREFUSED` while green — so the proxy errors are ambient (unmocked calls falling through to a backend that is not there by design) and are *not* the regression. The regression is the un-skipping.

Reverting the key restores the pre-existing false positive in `e2e-isolation-coverage`, which asserts credentials are present while the specs still skip. That is stated rather than hidden: it is a **non-required** check, it is what WIC-2122/WIC-2199 already track, and an undeployable `main` outranks it. Re-enabling the specs needs a backend in CI, not a credential; the honest interim gate is an explicit `E2E_LIVE_BACKEND` opt-in on the specs themselves (WIC-2199 §2), which changes test-gating semantics across four files and wants its own review.

### Tested — the two interview-date render sites a design ruling recorded as "permanently dark" are now asserted to be lit (2026-09-06)

`docs/design/SAVED_FILTER_SHORTCUT_NAMING.md` (WIC-1775 via WIC-1812) recorded two dead-code findings alongside its ruling. The first: `InterviewPrepPage` read `application.interviewDate` off a type with no such property, so the value was always `undefined` and *"the interview-date render sites in `InterviewPrepCard.tsx` and `QuickReferenceExport.tsx` are permanently dark."* WIC-2023 put `interviewDate` on the prep endpoint's `ApplicationSummary`, which lit both — and nothing had looked at them since. `git ls-tree | grep -i interviewprep` returned **no test file at all**, so "they work now" was a source reading rather than a measurement. This is the measurement (WIC-2192).

**The test sits at the page, and that placement is the whole point.** `applicationSummary` copies four fields and deliberately omits `interviewDate`; both consumers are handed `{ ...applicationSummary, interviewDate: application.interviewDate }`, so one explicit override per site is the entire wiring. Delete either and that site goes dark again **with no type error** — the target property is optional on both prop types, which is exactly why `tsc` did not catch the original defect and would not catch its return. A test rendering `InterviewPrepCard` directly with an `interviewDate` prop would pass against that deletion: it would assert the component's formatting, one layer below the wiring that was broken. Confirmed by mutation rather than asserted: dropping the card-site override reds 3 of 6 and leaves the export site green; dropping the export-site override reds exactly 1 and leaves the card green. The two sites fail independently because they are two sites.

**The timezone is pinned, and the box this ran on proves it had to be.** Both sites format an *instant* through `toLocaleDateString`, which resolves against the host zone, and this repo pins `TZ` nowhere. The chosen instant — `2026-09-10T02:30:00.000Z` — lands on **different calendar days** either side of the date line: the evening of the 9th in `America/New_York`, the morning of the 10th in `Asia/Tokyo`. Removing the pins and running under `TZ=UTC` (which is what this box is set to, and what CI is) reds 3 of 6. The Tokyo case is a control rather than a second copy of the same measurement: it is what reds a future "simplification" to `interviewDate.slice(0, 10)`, which prints the 10th in every zone on earth. Verified — that mutant reds exactly the two zone assertions and nothing else.

**The unscheduled case is asserted too, because `NULL` is the common row.** Every application predating WIC-2023 has no interview date, and `new Date(undefined)` formats as `Invalid Date` rather than throwing, so a guard testing the wrong thing fails silently and visibly at once. The export-preview negative control matches on `weekday: 'long'` rather than on the year: that dialog's footer already carries an unrelated *"Generated with Careerpin • 9/6/2026"*, which is today's date and therefore drifts, and a year-matching sweep reds on the footer instead of on the site under test. That was not reasoned out in advance — the first draft matched the year and failed for exactly that reason.

No production code changes. The naming ruling itself is untouched and `constants/filterShortcuts.test.ts` still enforces it; whether the "Interviews This Week" shortcut should now be wired up and renamed is a separate product decision, open on WIC-2192.


### Documentation — the product-name do-not-sweep list named a file that no longer matches, and omitted the largest surviving concentration (2026-09-06)

`CONTENT_STYLE.md`'s Exception 1 tells a future product-name sweep what to leave alone. Three of its claims had gone stale, all in the safe direction, which is why nothing broke and why nobody noticed (WIC-1954 follow-up).

It reported **18 occurrences across 15 files** still awaiting cleanup in the root `README.md`, `packages/api/`, `docs/architecture/` and `docs/analytics/`. Measured at `f1c01273`: **zero remain in all four paths** — that sweep ran, and the document went on presenting it as outstanding work. It also listed `e2e/auth.spec.ts` among the deliberate historical records; the file exists, the string does not, so the list was protecting nothing there.

**The omission is the one that mattered.** `.gitleaks-baseline.json` holds **14 occurrences, the largest concentration outside `CHANGELOG.md`**, and it was on no list at all. A baseline quotes historical content by design — editing it invalidates the baseline and re-opens every finding it acknowledges — so it is squarely a do-not-sweep class, and it was the one class a sweep would have hit first and understood least.

Replaced the prose list with a four-class table and a `git grep -c` derivation, on the rule that a file the command prints and the table does not is either a new occurrence or a new class. Counts in this note rot — twice now — so the note no longer carries one. Same reasoning as the changelog-count guidance in `CLAUDE.md`. No rule changed and no string moved; this is the enforcement list catching up to the tree.


### Fixed — a blank `HOST` bound the dev API to every interface instead of loopback, in the one configuration where auth is bypassed (2026-09-06)

`config.ts` resolved the bind address with `process.env.HOST ?? '127.0.0.1'`. `??` falls back only on `null`/`undefined`, so a **present-but-empty** `HOST` won the coalesce as `''` and `index.ts` handed it to `serve({ hostname })`. Node reads an empty host as *unspecified* and binds the wildcard: measured, `host: ''` yields `{"address":"::","family":"IPv6"}` — dual-stack, so IPv4 too — against `{"address":"127.0.0.1"}` for the default. Loopback-only becomes every interface, with no error, no warning, and a startup banner that just prints `http://:::3000` (WIC-2197).

**Neither half is a defect; the composition is.** `HOST` is read only on the Node entry — local dev and self-host — which is the same configuration in which `middleware/auth.ts` takes its ADR-010 D3 bypass and serves every request as `LOCAL_DEV_USER_ID_DEFAULT`, the sentinel `migrations/0017` backfilled every pre-tenancy row to. So a blank `HOST` publishes an **unauthenticated, full-legacy-tenant API to the local network**. The bypass is deliberate and unchanged; what changes is that it can no longer be reached from off-box by accident.

**Blank is the shape this repo invites.** `.env.example` ships `HOST=127.0.0.1` and `index.ts` imports `dotenv/config`; editing that line to `HOST=` — the natural way to write "just use the default" — sets present-but-empty. The user's edit means *default*; the old code heard *all interfaces*. The example file now says so at the line itself.

**The fix is `||`, deliberately not the `?.trim() ||` idiom two fields below it** — the same call WIC-2191 made on `SUPABASE_URL`, for the same reason and with the same regression pin. A whitespace-only `HOST` is truthy, so it passes through and Node rejects it with `ENOTFOUND` — fail-**closed**. Trimming would collapse it to `''` and route it straight into the wildcard bind, moving the one input that fails safely into the unsafe direction.

**`PORT` had the same coercion bug in the opposite direction, and is fixed as diagnosability rather than safety.** `parseInt(process.env.PORT ?? '3000', 10)` maps blank to `NaN`, which `serve()` rejects with `ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT: options.port should be >= 0 and < 65536. Received type number (NaN)` — a message that never names `PORT`. It failed loud, so nothing was ever exposed by it; it just cost the operator a Node-internal socket error for a one-character `.env` slip. Blank now resolves to the documented default and a non-blank invalid value throws naming the variable. Same family as WIC-2183 (`Number('')` is `0`).

**Scope correction to WIC-2191's own note.** That entry recorded *"the card's sweep of the other `??`-guarded config fields was re-checked and holds — every other consumer tests them with truthiness, so blank and absent already behave identically there."* Sound for the `string | null` fields, whose consumers are truthiness tests. `host` and `port` are not among them: their consumer is `serve()`, which tests neither, and for which blank and absent emphatically differ. This closes that gap.

**Graded by watching the tests fail first.** 14 new cases in `test/config-bind.test.ts`; against the unfixed coercion **6 fail**, and the 8 that pass are the positive controls (configured and absent values, which behave identically either way, as they must). `packages/api` is 89 files / 1716 tests green, against a 88 / 1702 baseline on `origin/main` — exactly conserved. `tsc -p packages/api` clean.


### Added — an interview date can now be entered, so the interview-prep countdown finally has something to count down to (2026-09-06)

`applications.interview_date` shipped end to end on the API side in WIC-2023 — column, create, update, DTO — and the two surfaces that read it (`InterviewPrepCard`'s countdown and the exported quick reference in `QuickReferenceExport`) were already built and tested. Nothing wrote to it. Every row was `NULL`, so both render sites were permanently dark. This adds the missing writer: the field on the web `Application` and `ApplicationFormData` models, the three hand-written mapper sites between them and the wire, and a labelled control in the form's Extended Tracking block (WIC-2188).

**The control is `datetime-local`, and copying the field beside it would have been wrong.** `nextActionDue` sits in the same block and is a `date` input validated `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$`; `interviewDate` is a `TIMESTAMPTZ` the API validates as `z.string().datetime({ offset: true })`. Three plausible implementations are all rejected by the API with a 400: a `date` input's `2026-09-10`, a `datetime-local` input's raw `2026-09-10T14:30` (no seconds, no offset), and the same value with seconds but still no zone. The form therefore converts on submit and back on prefill, in `utils/datetimeLocal.ts`, and the conversion is a module with its own suite rather than two inline expressions because **both directions have a wrong-looking-right one-liner**: `new Date('2026-09-10')` is a perfectly valid `Date` read as UTC midnight, and `iso.slice(0, 16)` is a perfectly valid `datetime-local` value showing the UTC wall clock. Neither is a crash; both are a silently wrong instant.

**Clearing a scheduled date was predicted, not measured, and is now measured.** The card that specified this work flagged its own AC-4 as an unverified prediction — that sending `''` would land as `NULL` because the update route's `.transform(v => v === '' ? undefined : v)` leaves the *key present* while `application.service.ts` writes on `if ('interviewDate' in input)`. That is a claim about zod's key-retention semantics with no type-level consequence whatsoever (`{ interviewDate: undefined }` and `{}` have the same TypeScript type), which is exactly why nothing had caught it either way. `packages/api/test/application-interview-date.write.test.ts` runs the real route, schema, service and a real Postgres (PGlite with the project's migrations replayed) and confirms it: **`''` clears the column, and omitting the key leaves it alone.** The `null`-sending workaround the card held in reserve is not needed. The second half of that sentence is the control — an implementation that wrote `NULL` on every PATCH would satisfy the clear case on its own.

**Every new test pins `process.env.TZ`, and that is the point rather than a detail.** The whole defect class here is offsets, and in UTC a broken implementation and a correct one differ by exactly zero. This repo pins no timezone (`TZ` is absent from `vitest.config.ts` and from `src/test/setup.ts`), so the ambient zone on CI is UTC and an unpinned suite would have been green against the raw-value and ISO-slice implementations alike. The suites set `America/New_York`, assert literal instants, and carry an `Asia/Tokyo` case as the negative control — a date-line crossing an ISO slice gets wrong by a whole day, not merely by an hour. A pure round-trip assertion is present too, and is explicitly labelled as necessary-but-not-sufficient: the slice implementation satisfies it.

**Where the date-only regression is asserted.** No `datetime-local` control can emit `2026-09-10`, so the DOM path cannot reach the regression the API's WIC-2023 comment warns about. `applicationFormSchema` is the layer that would readmit it — swap the rule for its neighbour's and the form still renders and still submits — so the schema is asserted directly as well as through the rendered control, with a positive control alongside so "rejects a date alone" cannot be satisfied by a rule that rejects everything. The schema moved to its own module in the process: it is the first rule on this form that *transforms* rather than merely validating, which makes it worth testing directly, and `react-refresh/only-export-components` is an error in this package.

Out of scope by the card's own division, and still open: the list-endpoint date-range filter and `sortBy: 'interviewDate'` (slice (b), blocked on this), and any "Interviews This Week" saved-filter shortcut, which stays gated behind `docs/design/SAVED_FILTER_SHORTCUT_NAMING.md`.


### Fixed — a "prefer this hook" docstring that both of its callers ignored is now a property of the API instead (2026-09-06)

`useApplications`' docstring directed callers to `useApplicationCollection` on *"any surface that renders a count, a total, or a 'nothing to see here' conclusion"*, because `truncated` is the only signal that the rows are a prefix of the account rather than the whole of it. It had exactly two callers and **both broke that rule**: `components/CommandPalette.tsx` rendered "No results found", and `App.tsx` rendered the nav count badges. This entry supersedes the *"Recorded and deliberately not actioned"* paragraph in the WIC-2179 entry below, which is where the finding was first written down (WIC-2181).

**The decision was not obviously "migrate", and it is worth recording why it went that way.** The alternative on the table was to narrow the docstring — a contract nothing enforces and every caller violates is worse than no contract, because the next reader takes it for a guarantee. Three facts settled it:

- **The migration costs nothing at the data layer.** `useApplications` was `useApplicationCollection` with `select: (c) => c.applications` bolted on: _same_ `queryKey`, _same_ `queryFn`, same cache entry. Switching a call site adds no request and no cache key — it changes only whether the rows arrive inside their metadata or stripped of it.
- **Migrating both left the hook with zero callers.** Its only remaining function would have been to _withhold_ the completeness signal from whoever called it next. It is therefore deleted, which turns the docstring's request into a property of the only list API there is. The module keeps every other export.
- **The contract could not honestly be narrowed to exclude counts.** `pages/ApplicationsList.tsx` already honours the count half in shipped code, with a notice reading _"Showing the first N of M applications. The counts below cover only what is shown"_. Excluding counts would have contradicted behaviour already on `main`.

**What the two surfaces now say.** The palette gains a third incomplete-results state alongside the in-flight and failed ones WIC-2179 added, in both places those are rendered: the empty branch says _"No matches among the first N of your M applications — the rest were not searched"_ instead of "No results found", and a non-empty result list carries the inline notice _"Only the first N of your M applications were searched…"_. The nav badge renders **"12+"** rather than "12", the `+` `aria-hidden` beside an `sr-only` " or more" — the hidden-glyph-plus-spoken-replacement shape WIC-1850 established, because screen readers disagree about whether to announce punctuation and a listener must not hear a floor as an exact figure.

**Scope stated honestly: this fires for nobody.** `truncated` requires `MAX_APPLICATION_PAGES` (50) × `APPLICATION_PAGE_SIZE` (100) = **5,000** applications for a single user. Unlike WIC-2179, which fired on every cold load and every failed request, there is no user reaching this today. It is fixed because the honest branch costs less than the paragraph explaining why the dishonest one is tolerable.

**Graded against the defect, with no 5,000-row fixture and no hook mock.** A fixture of 5,000 rows would measure the fixture generator; a mocked hook handing back `{ truncated: true }` would leave the migration itself untested, since a mocked hook is satisfied by any hook name. `CommandPalette.truncated.test.tsx` (5 cases) therefore drives the real `useApplicationCollection` through a real `QueryClient` and stubs one layer lower at `applicationService.getAllPaged`, serving **one** row while reporting a `totalCount` of 137 — the two disagree on purpose, so an assertion cannot pass by reading the wrong one. Two of the five are negative controls holding everything constant but `truncated`, and a fifth pins the precondition that the fixture rows reach the component at all. `navigation-lower-bound-badge.test.tsx` (6 cases) covers both nav surfaces, since they render the badge from separate copies of the same markup; each pairs the visible reading with the announced one, because `toHaveTextContent` sees `aria-hidden` nodes and alone cannot tell "12+" from "12+ or more". `App.navBadgeTruncation.test.tsx` (9 cases) pins the wiring `App.tsx` cannot be rendered to test, and says in its own docstring what a source scan cannot catch.


### Added — a keyboard-nav suite named for a route now has to name a route the app renders (2026-09-06)

`test/reportsKeyboardNav.tsx`'s `renderReportPage(page, path)` does not look `path` up in `App.tsx`. It **synthesizes** the route from its own two arguments — `<MemoryRouter initialEntries={[path]}><Routes><Route path={path} element={page} />` — so the path string is a **label, not a route lookup**, and a suite written against a path the app sends somewhere else is green and stays green. It asserts a conditional (*"if `/x` rendered this component, its cards would be keyboard-reachable"*) whose antecedent nothing checks (WIC-2190).

**That is not hypothetical, and it already cost real work.** WIC-2062 fixed bare-div navigation on "four Reports* pages". Three of the four are live routes; the fourth, `/reports/pipeline`, is `<Navigate to="/applications" replace />` at `App.tsx:137-140` — so a quarter of that dispatch shipped to a page no user can open, its suite has been green over it since, and the page counted as covered in the a11y accounting. `routeOutline.render.test.tsx` already knew the route was dead (it is listed in that file's `NOT_A_RENDERED_ROUTE`); the keyboard-nav suites simply never consulted that knowledge. `test/keyboardNavRouteCoverage.test.ts` is the missing link, and it deliberately mirrors the older check's shape: the exclusions are **data**, so adding one is a reviewable edit rather than a silent narrowing.

**Built so it can fail, because every assertion in it reports a defect by returning an empty list** — the failure mode this repo has measured before (WIC-1903), where a rule with no findings is indistinguishable from a rule that reports nothing. The scope, the extraction and the classifier each carry their own positive control: `classifyRoute` is pinned on **both** answers against the real `App.tsx` (a version returning `'renders-a-component'` unconditionally would make every downstream assertion pass), the glob is pinned to contain the four known suites, and the path regex is asserted to extract from every suite it finds. Four synthetic cases then require the guard to actually report a redirected route, an undeclared route, and — the differential — to *clear* a live one, so it is not simply always-red. Verified by mutation rather than by inspection: dropping the single exclusion turns the tree red with exactly `ReportsPipeline.keyboardNav.test.tsx covers /reports/pipeline — navigates-away`, and the other 14 cases stay green.

**The exclusion is asserted to still be earned.** An allowlist nobody re-checks is how the next unrouted page gets a green suite, so the entry is invalid the moment `/reports/pipeline` is wired up: the check reads the excluded suite's own path back out of `App.tsx` and fails if it now renders, telling you to drop the entry.

**`ReportsPipeline.tsx` is annotated rather than deleted, and the reason is mechanical.** `constants/stale.drift.test.ts` imports it as `?raw` and pins it in a **scope control** (`expect(FILES).toContain('/src/pages/ReportsPipeline.tsx')`) plus three provenance assertions. A `?raw` import of a missing module is a **build-time** failure, so deleting the page does not turn one test red — it stops the whole suite loading, `Tests no tests`, measured rather than assumed. The dead page has become a live test fixture. Whether a pipeline report should exist as a product remains open in WIC-1100 and is not settled here; both the page and its keyboard-nav suite now carry headers saying they are component coverage, not route coverage.


### Fixed — the command palette no longer reports "No results found" for a search it has not finished, or could not run at all (2026-09-06)

`components/CommandPalette.tsx` read only `data` from `useApplications()` and defaulted it to `[]`. react-query leaves `data` `undefined` **both** while a query is in flight **and** when it has failed, so that one default collapsed three distinct states into a single empty array — *"we don't know yet"*, *"we couldn't find out"*, and *"there are genuinely none"* — which the results region rendered as the flat claim **"No results found"** (WIC-2179).

**The measurement**, with the node named so it can be re-run — an earlier draft of this entry said "byte-identical across all 1546 characters" without saying *what* was measured, which made the number unreproducible. The node is the palette's `role="dialog"` subtree, measured at base `66ae5778` with the user's own typed query held constant (two queries of equal length, Radix's per-mount generated ids normalised). Its **announced text** — every `aria-hidden` subtree stripped, i.e. what actually reaches the user — was **234 characters for *"an application that exists, still loading"* and the identical 234 characters for *"a query that genuinely matches nothing"*: zero differing characters.** For reference the raw markup of that same node was 1540 characters of `innerHTML` / 2162 of `outerHTML`, differing in 13 — all of them inside the search input's own `value`, the user's keystrokes rather than anything the palette was telling them. The announced-text identity is the figure that matters and the one carrying no caveat, and it is now a permanent assertion rather than a one-off probe.

**The error half is not a flash, and it is why this is graded above cosmetic.** The palette opens on Cmd+K, deliberately and fast, typically the instant a page becomes usable — so the in-flight window is exactly when it is used. But `isError` leaves `data` `undefined` *permanently*: a user whose applications request failed was told, for as long as they left the palette open and with no other signal anywhere in the component, that they had no matching applications.

**A second surface, where the empty state never renders at all.** Typing `Applied` — a `SUGGESTED_FILTERS` title — matches a suggestion, so the result list is *non-empty*: the palette looks confident and complete while every one of the user's actual applications is silently missing, and the empty-state branch is never reached. Fixing only the empty state would have left this case still lying, so a partial list now carries an inline notice naming what is absent from it.

The honest empty state is unchanged.

Both new strings carry `role="status"`, and the limit of that is stated rather than implied: it **exposes** them as a status region but does **not** reliably get them **announced**, because the empty-state element unmounts the moment any result appears, and a freshly-mounted live region is announced inconsistently across screen readers — which is exactly why this repo's shared announcer (WIC-1794) is mounted permanently instead. Routing these strings through that announcer was considered and deliberately deferred: it portals to `<body>`, and the palette is a Radix modal whose `hideOthers` hides everything outside its own content, so the migration is real work rather than a one-line swap. The role is a strict improvement on the bare `<p>` that was there, and it is not load-bearing for the defect.

**Scope was swept, not assumed.** All 32 query-hook call sites in `packages/web/src` were classified; four read `data` with no loading state, and only this one produces a false claim. `App.tsx:76,77` renders nav badges only at `count > 0`, so in-flight is an *absent* badge rather than a wrong one; `onboarding/OnboardingModal.tsx:60` is self-healing, because `PersonalInfoForm` resets the form in a `useEffect` when `personalInfo` arrives. Both are recorded as checked rather than left unexplained.

**Recorded and deliberately not actioned:** `useApplications`' own docstring directs callers to `useApplicationCollection` on *"any surface that renders a count, a total, or a 'nothing to see here' conclusion"*, since only that hook surfaces `truncated`. This component and `App.tsx` both violate that contract. It is unreachable in practice — `truncated` requires `MAX_APPLICATION_PAGES` (50) × `APPLICATION_PAGE_SIZE` (100) = **5,000** applications — so it is documented here rather than fixed, and wants its own card if the contract is to be enforced rather than merely described.

**`isPending`, not `isLoading` — the third instance of this same defect, caught in review.** The first version of this fix read `isLoading || isError`. In react-query v5 `isLoading` is `isPending && isFetching`, so a query that is **pending but paused** — `fetchStatus: "paused"`, which is exactly what the default `networkMode: "online"` does the moment the browser reports itself offline — has `isLoading` false, `isError` false, and `data` still `undefined`. The `= []` default fired and the palette rendered `🔍 No results found`, byte-for-byte the pre-fix output. It is production-reachable: `networkMode` is set nowhere in `packages/web/src`, and the only production `QueryClient` (`main.tsx`) sets just `retry` / `refetchOnWindowFocus` / `staleTime`. `isPending` covers every state in which `data` is `undefined` and the query has not failed.

**Graded against the defect.** Eight new tests in `CommandPalette.loadingState.test.tsx`, of which **three are negative controls**: the honest empty state must survive (without it, "delete the empty state" passes every other test in the file), no notice may appear once settled, and the no-query landing view must be unaffected. The existing `CommandPalette.test.tsx` stays 12/12; its `vi.mock` now states `isPending: false, isError: false` explicitly, having previously got the settled state right only by the accident of `undefined` being falsy.

**And a second test file, because the first one structurally cannot catch the paused state.** `CommandPalette.loadingState.test.tsx` mocks the hook and derives `data` from the same flags the component branches on, so `data === undefined ⟺ isPending || isError` holds there *by construction* — it asserts the fix's own premise rather than testing it, and a fourth boolean on the mock would only have renamed that problem. `CommandPalette.pausedQuery.test.tsx` therefore mocks no hook at all: it drives the real `useApplications` through a real `QueryClient` with `onlineManager` forced offline, asserts the reached state is genuinely `pending`/`paused` with the fetch never started, and pairs each offline assertion with the same query run online. Reverting `isPending` to `isLoading` kills two of its four tests on the literal string `No results found`; the mocked file's failures under that same mutant are only a missing-flag artifact and do not count as kills. The docstring on that mock now records its limit instead of claiming it "models the real hook".



### Added — the applications list can be filtered to an interview-date window and sorted by it, with NULLS LAST pinned in both directions (2026-09-06)

`applications.interview_date` has been a real, writable column since WIC-2023, but the list endpoint could neither filter nor sort on it: `listQuerySchema` carried `status`/`company`/`search`/`sortBy`/`sortOrder`/`limit`/`page` and nothing date-shaped, and the `sortBy` enum was `['createdAt','updatedAt','company']` (WIC-2189).

- **Two new query params, `interviewDateFrom` and `interviewDateTo`**, inclusive on both ends, composing with the existing filters rather than replacing them. Both take `z.string().datetime({ offset: true })` — the contract WIC-2023 established for this column — and **not** the `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` regex `nextActionDue` uses. That is the one real design choice here: the column is `TIMESTAMPTZ` and the service hands these straight to `new Date(...)`, so a date-only bound would be read as UTC midnight and shift the window by up to a day for any caller west of Greenwich. It is the identical hazard `routes/applications.ts:54-57` already documents for the request body, arriving through a query string instead.
- **`sortBy: 'interviewDate'`, with `NULLS LAST` written into the SQL on both directions rather than inherited.** Postgres defaults to `NULLS LAST` for `ASC` but `NULLS FIRST` for `DESC`, so a plain `DESC` would open the list with every application that has *no* interview scheduled. Most rows are `NULL` and will stay that way for a long time, so the default does not merely misplace a few rows — it fills the entire first page with exactly the applications the sort was meant to push aside, and does it in only one of the two directions. An implementation that leans on `desc(col)` alone therefore passes every `ASC` assertion and fails only on `DESC`, which is why the two directions are asserted separately.
- **A `NULL` interview date is excluded by either bound, not sorted to an end.** A comparison against `NULL` is `NULL`, never true, so unscheduled applications fall out of a windowed query on their own. That is the intended reading — "applications interviewing between X and Y" does not include the ones that are not interviewing at all — and it is pinned by its own test so the filter semantics cannot be quietly conflated with the ordering rule.
- **`applications.id` is a load-bearing tiebreaker on the interview-date sort, not decoration.** The `NULL` block is large and every row in it compares equal on the sort key, so its internal order is unspecified; offset pagination issues one query per page, and Postgres is free to order an equal-ranked block differently between them, which silently drops some rows and repeats others. A unique trailing key makes the total order deterministic. The paging test walks all five pages of a 17-row fixture and asserts each id appears exactly once — with the tiebreaker removed it fails, along with three others.
- **An inverted range is a 400, not a silent empty page.** Left to the database, `from > to` is a well-formed query that matches nothing, which a caller cannot distinguish from "no interviews scheduled". A schema-level refinement rejects it before the service is reached. An empty bound (`?interviewDateFrom=`, what an unfilled form control serialises to) is still treated as absent, matching the sibling fields.

**Graded against a real Postgres, and every assertion mutation-tested.** The 12 filter/sort cases run against PGlite with the project's real migrations replayed in `_journal.json` order, not against a query stub — each claim under test is a property of the emitted SQL rather than of the TypeScript around it, and a stub that returns rows in the order the test wants proves only that the test author knew the answer. Six mutations were run against the finished implementation, each reverting one decision: removing `NULLS LAST` from the `DESC` branch fails 3 cases, dropping the id tiebreaker fails 4, `gte`→`gt` fails 1, deleting the upper bound fails 2, relaxing the `datetime` contract fails 2, and dropping the range refinement fails 1. Every run kept `passed + failed` equal to the baseline, so no mutant went green by failing to compile.

**Deliberately not in scope.** The "Interviews This Week" saved-filter shortcut stays gated behind `docs/design/SAVED_FILTER_SHORTCUT_NAMING.md`, and `packages/web/src/constants/filterShortcuts.test.ts` still rejects time-word labels — that rule was WIC-1775's original finding and relaxing it is a separate, deliberate decision, never a side effect of shipping a filter. `FilterPanel`'s `dateRange` control filters "Date added / applied" (`appliedAt`/`createdAt`), a different window, and is untouched. No web-side control is added here; the `datetime-local` control that populates the column from the UI landed separately in WIC-2188, which is what makes this filter operate over rows that can actually carry a value rather than over an all-`NULL` column.

### Fixed — a blank `DB_CONNECT_DEADLINE_MS` armed a 0 ms connect deadline, counterfeiting the data-plane outage on a healthy database (2026-09-06)

`resolveConnectDeadlineMs` (`packages/api/src/db/connect-bound.ts`) returned the default for `undefined` and for anything `Number()` could not parse, but `Number('')` is **`0`** — and `0` is not a rejected value here, it is the most aggressive *valid* setting, arming the watchdog on the first macrotask. So a blank override did not fall back; it selected an immediate trip. `tripDbCircuit` then tore the pool down and opened the per-request circuit, and every DB-touching request in the Worker answered `503` with `Database unreachable: no connection could be established` — against a database that was entirely healthy. Measured on the resolver as it stood: `''`, `' '`, `'\n'` and `'\t '` all resolved to **0**, where `'not-a-number'` and `'-1'` correctly resolved to 1500 (WIC-2183).

**Why blank is the realistic shape of the misconfiguration, not a contrived one.** A GitHub Actions expression for a secret that does not exist expands to the empty string, and `wrangler secret put` then stores it and prints `✨ Success!`. This repo has already been bitten by exactly that and written it down: `set-worker-secrets.yml` records `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` going empty on run 33972091515 for precisely this reason. There the cost is a silently disabled feature. Here it would have been a total, self-inflicted outage wearing the symptoms of an upstream one.

**That last part is what grades this above a validation nit.** The string a 0 ms deadline produces is byte-identical to what the live WIC-2092 data-plane fault emits, down to `connect deadline exceeded` in `/api/health` — the surface the fleet is actively reading to diagnose that incident. A one-character config slip would have been indistinguishable from the outage under investigation, and would have pointed every reader upstream at Supabase, which is the one place the fault would not have been.

**The same trap, already documented and defended one directory over.** `lib/pagination.ts` carries it verbatim from WIC-1308 — *"`Number('')` is `0`, so a cursor decoding to nothing would silently mean page one — the failure mode being fixed, just quieter"* — and guards with a digits test. This resolver was the copy that never got the guard. `types/env.ts` meanwhile already promised the behaviour that was missing (*"an unparseable value falls back to it"*), so the declared contract and the code disagreed; the comment now states the blank case explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred.

**Latent, and reported as latent.** No workflow sets `DB_CONNECT_DEADLINE_MS` today — it is `undefined` in production, so the default has always been in force and nothing shipped was ever affected. This closes the footgun before the var is first used, which given ADR-007's standing `⛔ Do not raise DB_CONNECT_DEADLINE_MS` is the likeliest moment for someone to reach for it.

**The fix rejects blank rather than rejecting zero**, which is the tempting shorter version: three cases in `db-connect-bound.test.ts` arm an immediate trip with an explicit `'0'`, so making blank default by outlawing zero would have removed that escape hatch. `'0'` still means zero and is now pinned by an assertion saying so. `trim()` rather than `=== ''` because a value routed through a shell or a YAML block can arrive as a lone newline, and `Number('\n')` is `0` too.

**Graded by watching the tests fail first.** Three new cases — the resolver unit, plus an end-to-end case on *both* Workers branches (`DATABASE_URL` and `HYPERDRIVE`) asserting `ctx.dbUnreachable` is still unset 150 ms into a blank-override request. Against the unfixed resolver all three fail, the end-to-end pair on a real `DatabaseUnreachableError`; against the fix the file is 24/24. Both branches are covered deliberately: they build their pools through the same `createWorkersPool`, so a fix applied to one path only would still have passed a single-branch test.


### Fixed — a blank `SUPABASE_URL` + `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` opened the local-dev auth bypass above the token check (2026-09-06)

`middleware/auth.ts` resolved both of its gate inputs with `??`, which falls back only on `null`/`undefined`. A Worker binding that is **present but empty** therefore won the coalesce as `''` — which is falsy, so `!supabaseUrl && !jwtSecret` read TRUE and the local-dev bypass fired, `return next()`-ing *above* the `Authorization: Bearer` check. The request needed no token at all, in a deployment whose `SUPABASE_*` config was set correctly the whole time. Both are now `||`, so blank falls through to the configured value; `config.ts` normalises the same two env vars the same way (WIC-2191).

**What it granted is worse than anonymous.** The bypass supplies `LOCAL_DEV_USER_ID_DEFAULT` = `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`, which `migrations/0017_enforce_userid_not_null.sql` backfilled every pre-tenancy `user_id` to, and `app.ts:127` is `api.use('*', authMiddleware)` — so an unauthenticated caller would read and write as the tenant owning every legacy row, on every API route. Confirmed by test rather than by reading: presenting a **valid** token for `user-blank-binding` against blank bindings, the service was invoked with `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`.

**Latent, and reported as latent.** No shipped deployment is affected and no path to one was found. `deploy.yml`'s `Validate required secrets` step `exit 1`s on `[ -z "$SUPABASE_URL" ]` / `[ -z "$SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET" ]` in both the preview and production jobs, `wrangler.jsonc` sets no `SUPABASE_*` var in either environment, and `set-worker-secrets.yml` only ever writes `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. What earns the fix is that **the guard lives in a workflow, not in the code** — a manual `wrangler secret put`, a new workflow, or `remediate-worker-secret-leak.yml` bypasses it entirely — and that the failure direction is fail-**open**. WIC-2183 was the same coercion class and failed loud, to a 503; this one produces no error, no log line, and a 200. Blank is also the documented realistic shape: an Actions expression for a missing secret expands to the empty string and `wrangler secret put` stores it and prints `Success`, already observed here on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in run 33972091515.

**The fix is `||`, deliberately not the `?.trim() ||` idiom sitting two lines below it.** That idiom is correct at `:77` for `LOCAL_DEV_USER_ID`, where the fallback is a safe sentinel, and wrong on the gate, where the fallback decides whether auth runs at all: `'   '` is truthy, so a whitespace-only binding takes the JWT path and 401s — fail-closed. Trimming would collapse it to `''`, fall through to an absent config and open the very bypass this closes. `deploy.yml`'s guard is `[ -z "$X" ]`, which **passes** a whitespace-only secret, so trimming would move the one input CI cannot catch from the safe direction to the unsafe one. Not trimming also leaves `jwtSecret` untouched as HS256 key material. A regression test pins whitespace-only as fail-closed so the "tidier" version cannot be reintroduced.

**When the bypass fires is otherwise unchanged.** Absent-both still bypasses — that is ADR-010 D3's local-dev/E2E path, and the middleware comment at `:69-72` is explicit that the condition is deliberate. This collapses *blank* into *absent-in-the-binding* so the config fallback gets its turn; it does not tighten the gate, and two cases pin that (blank-both-with-no-config, and absent-both) alongside a positive control asserting the configured secret still authenticates a real token.

**Scope note, correcting the card.** The card asked for the same fix on `plugins/auth.ts` "one level up". That file is dead code and could not be covered as asked: nothing imports `authPlugin`, `src/plugins` is in `tsconfig.json`'s `exclude`, and `fastify`/`fastify-plugin` are not dependencies, so it cannot even be imported by a test. The `config.ts` half is still made, because `getConfig()` is the fallback side of every live `c.env?.X ?? getConfig().x` call site and its declared `string | null` was not honest about `''`. The card's sweep of the other `??`-guarded config fields was re-checked and holds — every other consumer tests them with truthiness, so blank and absent already behave identically there.

### Fixed — the last reload-class navigation is now a router call, and a lint rule keeps the class at zero (2026-09-06)

`pages/ResumeManager.tsx:164` sent the "Upload Your First Resume" empty-state action through `window.location.href = '/resumes/upload'` — a document navigation that tears down the page, discards the React Query cache and re-downloads the bundle to render a view the router reaches in place. It is now `navigate('/resumes/upload')`. `useNavigate` was already imported and `const navigate = useNavigate()` already existed at `:28` (used at `:111` for `/catalog`), so the fix is one token in an idiom the file already established (WIC-1097).

**This closes a class that was orphaned by a ticket that was never filed.** WIC-1068 AC3.2 removed the `ProjectDetail` instance and pointed the reader at *"WIC-1044's sibling ticket on reload-class navigation, filed alongside this one"*. That sibling does not exist on the board, so the class sat at exactly one survivor with no owner from 2026-08-19 to today. Rather than fix the site and leave the same gap behind, the change also lands `local/no-reload-navigation`, so the count cannot go back up.

**The rule resolves through scope analysis, not name matching.** `isWindowLocation` accepts a bare `location` only when it resolves to no declaration in any enclosing scope. Reads are not writes: `const url = window.location.href` and `window.location.pathname === '/'` navigate nowhere and are not flagged.

⚠️ **Corrected 2026-09-06 (WIC-2173) — the justification originally printed here was measurably false, and it is worth saying why rather than quietly deleting it.** This paragraph claimed the tree's `location.pathname` reads (22 of them across 11 files — `TopNavigation`, `BottomTabBar`, `MobileNavigation`, `ResumeManagerTabs`, `RouteTitle`, `NotFound`, `useRouteFocusHandoff` and several test harnesses) were what the scope analysis protected, because *"a rule that matched on the identifier's name would report all of them."* It would not. Force `isUnresolvedGlobal` to `return true` — pure name matching — and `npm run lint` on the unmodified tree is **rc=0 with zero findings**. The rule visits only `AssignmentExpression` and `CallExpression`, so a read never reaches the resolution step under *any* strategy; those 22 sites are excluded by reads-are-not-writes. The original name-matching mutant was consistent with this all along: it reds only *writes on local bindings*, which is a fact about the suite rather than about the tree.

⚠️ **The first draft of this correction said 35, and 35 was wrong — recorded because the error is the same class the paragraph above exists to fix.** `git grep -o 'location\.pathname' -- packages/web/src` returns 35, and that raw total was published as a count of *reads*. Hand-classified it is not one: it includes the rule test's own **write** fixtures — the exact sites the rule *does* flag, so counting them as reads it leaves alone is backwards — plus prose lines, two of which are the false sentence being corrected. The genuine figure is **22 reads across 11 files**, identical on `main` `70ab70e5` and on this branch. Note the entry this replaced said *"20+"*, which was **true**: a correct lower bound was swapped for an incorrect exact figure, in permanent text, by the change whose whole thesis is that permanent text must claim only what was measured. No conclusion moves either way — the load-bearing claim is that those sites are excluded by reads-are-not-writes, and that holds at any count.

**The real justification is narrower and sharper, and is now tested.** Scope analysis is what separates the global from a local binding named `location` that is written to, or that has `assign`/`replace` **called** on it — and that last case is an everyday idiom rather than a contrivance, because `String.prototype.replace` and `Location.prototype.replace` share a name. A local string named `location` with `location.replace(/^\//, '')` is string manipulation, and a name-matching rule reports it as navigation. Measured as a complementary pair in a real `src/services/*.ts` path: **shipped rule → not flagged; name-matching mutant → FLAGGED.** That is a genuine false positive the shipped rule avoids, and unlike the 22 reads it does not survive the mutant.

**`document.location` is now in scope (WIC-2173).** `document.location` is a documented alias for `window.location` — the same object — and a commoner spelling than either `globalThis` or `self`, both of which the rule accepted from the start. Omitting it was an oversight rather than a design line, so the object list is now `window` / `globalThis` / `self` / `document`. Zero sites on `main`, so the rule stays at zero findings and no `--max-warnings` ceiling moves. Widening the object list also widens what the scope analysis has to hold back, so a **local** binding named `document` is pinned as a negative case with its own control — realistic in a résumé-document app.

**The message no longer over-claims for `location.hash` (WIC-2173).** `hash` is in `NAVIGATING_PROPERTIES` and stays there — a hash write does set the URL behind the router's back — but it does **not** reload the document: it fires `hashchange` and scrolls, and the bundle, the document and the React Query cache all survive. The shared message asserted the opposite, in permanent text. `hash` now carries its own `hashNavigation` message describing what a hash write actually does, and a test pins both directions: the hash message must *not* say "reloads the whole document", and the `href` message must still say it.

**Graded against the defect, not merely observed green — the WIC-1903 hazard is the whole problem with this shape of change.** The rule lands at zero findings by design, and a rule reporting nothing at all is indistinguishable from a working one in any tree-state assertion: no-op the single `context.report(...)` in `no-literal-caps-jsx-text` and `caps-baseline.test.ts` stayed green, and so did `npm run lint`. Three controls were run instead:

Re-measured 2026-09-06 against the corrected suite, which is **39** tests (was 32). Every cell restored the file and re-greened afterwards:

- **Dead-rule mutant** — `if (false) context.report(…)` at all three report sites: **32 of 39** go red.
- **Name-matching mutant** — `isUnresolvedGlobal` forced to `true`: **5 of 39** go red — the three original react-router cases (the `useLocation()` write, the `location` parameter, the imported binding) plus the two added by WIC-2173, `.replace()` on a local string named `location` and the write to a local named `document`. ⚠️ Read this bullet as *the suite pins the scope analysis*, *not* as *the tree needs it*: the same mutant leaves `npm run lint` at rc=0 on the real tree (see the correction above).
- **Object-list mutant** — `document` removed from `LOCATION_OBJECTS`: **5 of 39** go red — the three `document.location` violating cases plus the two controls that depend on `document` still being read (the chained-gap control and the local-`document` control).
- **Hash-message mutant** — `hash` routed back to the shared `reloadNavigation` message: **exactly 1** goes red, and it is the assertion that the hash message does not claim a reload.
- **Real-tree positive controls (three)** — each applied to `ResumeManager.tsx:164` and reverted. Reverting to the pre-fix `window.location.href` fails `npm run lint` at `164:30` with the rule's own message; `document.location.href` at the same site also fails, which is what pins the widening against the real tree rather than only against synthetic snippets; and `window.location.hash` fails carrying the *corrected* message, naming `hashchange` and not claiming a reload.

Every "must not flag" case in the test carries a differential control — the same shape with the exempting feature removed, which must flag — so no `0 findings` assertion can be satisfied by a dead rule. The **four** KNOWN GAPS are pinned the same way rather than left as prose: `location.reload()` (a reload is not a navigation and has no router equivalent); a `location` reached through an alias or a computed member; a **chained** object expression (`window.document.location`, `window.top.location`), added by WIC-2173 because the object list is matched one level deep and `window.top` is a different document the router cannot reach at all; and `<a href>` / `<form action>`, which `route-integrity.test.ts` already reasons about as link sites. The chained gap was unlisted until WIC-2173 measured it — zero sites on `main`, so nothing was missed live, but this change's own thesis is that a gap should be deliberate rather than accidental.

**Off-site navigation is not special-cased in the rule, deliberately.** No router call leaves the origin, so `window.location.href = 'https://…'` is correct and the rule will flag it; the exemption belongs at the site as an `eslint-disable-next-line` carrying its reason, which is the convention this config already settled on for `jsx-a11y/no-autofocus`. Encoding "absolute URLs are fine" in the rule would silently permit `window.location.href = someVar` on the grounds that it *might* be off-site — the case most worth catching. Zero sites need the exemption today, and the escape hatch is named in the rule's message and pinned by a test.

Scope is `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`, matching `no-usestate-from-prop` rather than the caps rule's `tsx`: a `window.location` write is just as reachable from a service or a hook, and `services/` is where an auth redirect would most naturally be written. `error` with zero findings and no allowlist, so neither `--max-warnings` ceiling in `package.json` moves (WIC-2053 showed those are coupled to the a11y baselines).

**Not caught by the route-integrity audit, and never could be.** `/resumes/upload` is a live route with 10+ other link sites, so the audit had nothing to flag — and `navigate('/x')` is itself a credited link pattern, so the conversion leaves that audit's accounting unchanged.

### Added — the resume delete announcement is pinned in jsdom, not only in Playwright (2026-09-06)

Deleting a resume announces the outcome to a screen reader through a live region. Until now the only committed pin for that was `packages/web/e2e/modal-focus.spec.ts:413-467` — a browser-only test. Measured on PR #423 at `013da8d8`: removing the live region from `ResumeManager` outright left the **vitest** suite **fully green at 837/837**. `ResumeManager.outline.test.tsx` does render the page on both branches — injecting a throw reds both of its assertions — it simply grades heading levels, and a portalled `role="status"` is not a heading (WIC-2155). So the unit layer was blind to this behaviour entirely.

**Correction to this entry's original premise (WIC-2164).** As first written it claimed the e2e pin "has not executed on any PR or on `main`", because at that moment WIC-2131's deliberate loud-red gate failed `E2E Tests` at `Assert isolation-test credentials are present` and skipped `Run E2E tests` wholesale. WIC-2157 (PR #426) has since moved that assertion into its own non-required `e2e-isolation-coverage` job, and the e2e pin **runs and passes again** — verified on `main` at `813af9c9`, run `34014906059`, as test 115. This entry therefore records a second, faster layer, not a stand-in for a suppressed one. What remains credential-blocked is the isolation/RLS suite (WIC-2122, needs a human to mint `E2E_TEST_USER*`) — a different gap, which nothing here addresses.

`packages/web/src/pages/ResumeManager.announce.test.tsx` closes that gap in jsdom in ~4s.

**It counts writes rather than reading text, because reading the text cannot detect the defect.** Two resumes may legitimately share a filename — uploads dedupe on `contentHash`, not `fileName` — and after deleting the second one the region's text names the right file *either way*, since it is the first announcement still sitting there untouched. Only the sequence of writes separates the two worlds, so the test mirrors the e2e instrument: a `MutationObserver` on `body > [aria-live="polite"]`, filtered with that spec's own `/resume\.pdf.*deleted/i`. The page is driven through its real handlers — `handleDeleteClick` on open, `handleConfirmDelete` on confirm — over a resume list that actually shrinks through `resumeService`.

**Deliberately implementation-agnostic, so it survives PR #423.** Two mechanisms independently produce the second write and either alone suffices: `handleDeleteClick` clearing the region as the dialog opens, and `useAnnouncer`'s zero-width `REPEAT_MARKER`. `main` has the first; #423 migrates the page onto `<Announcer>`/`useAnnouncer` and has both. The test asserts the contract both serve — two deletes, two announcements — and both implementations render the region as `body > div[aria-live="polite"]`, so the **identical file passes unmodified on `main` and on #423's tree**, verified by replaying it onto `013da8d8`. It pins the outcome across that migration instead of whichever mechanism is in the file today, and is not a merge hazard for #423.

**Graded against the defect, not just observed green.** Removing the live region reds it (`live region not found`); removing the clear on `main` reds it at 1 write instead of 2, with the write sequence in the failure message. On #423's tree, removing the clear alone leaves it green — that is the redundancy in the production code, settled on #423 and consistent with the PR #326 / WIC-1918 ruling, and it is why only a two-mutant control discriminates there.

**The same-name fixture is load-bearing, and that was measured rather than asserted.** Re-run with distinct filenames, the clear-removed defect produces two genuinely different strings, mutates the region twice and **passes** — a distinct-name fixture is structurally blind to this bug. Two assertions the e2e spec makes are deliberately *not* copied: that the region sits outside `#root` and wraps nothing focusable are vacuous in jsdom, where Testing Library renders into a bare `<div>` on `document.body` and there is no `#root` at all. They stay in the e2e spec.

This does not reduce the need for WIC-2122. It adds a unit-layer guard to one behaviour that had none; the isolation/RLS coverage that WIC-2122 unblocks is untouched by it.

### Changed — `ResumeManager`'s delete announcer now uses the shared `Announcer`/`useAnnouncer` helper, and both announcements quote the name (2026-09-06)

`pages/ResumeManager.tsx` had a hand-rolled `createPortal(<div className="sr-only" aria-live="polite">…)` block doing the same job as the helper WIC-1304 extracted. It is now `<Announcer message={announcement} />` over `useAnnouncer()`, so the page contains no `createPortal` and no `aria-live` of its own and the portal/mounting rationale lives in one place instead of two. No user-visible change to the delete path (WIC-1794).

The `clear()` on dialog-open is **kept, with its rationale rewritten**. It previously existed to defeat React's `Object.is` bail on a repeated announcement — two resumes can share a `fileName`, since uploads dedupe on `contentHash`. `useAnnouncer.announce` now handles repeats internally by alternating an unspoken U+200B, so the clear survives only for the reason `ProjectsList` keeps it: not leaving a stale outcome in the accessibility tree while the user works on the next one.

⚠️ **The two mechanisms are now redundant on this path, and the e2e negative control can no longer isolate either one.** Measured as a 2×2 (`e2e/modal-focus.spec.ts` → "deleting a second identically-named resume announces it again, not silently"): real `announce` + clear → pass; **stubbed `announce` + clear → pass**; real `announce`, no clear → pass; stubbed `announce`, no clear → **fail**. The test goes red only when *both* are gone, because the clear writes `''` in a separate commit driven by a separate user action, so the following announcement is a real DOM change whether or not the marker logic runs. The repeat coverage did survive the migration — rows 3 and 4 show `announce` alone carries it — but a single-mutant control over `announce` is now vacuous here and should be stated as the two-mutant form.

`ProjectsList`'s create-success announcement now quotes the project name (`Project "Acme Corp" created.`), matching `Resume "resume.pdf" deleted.` and closing the non-blocking note left on PR #252: unquoted, a project named `created` or one ending in a period produced a sentence that is hard to parse aloud. Its two pinned assertions move with it.


### Documentation — the prod canary's green run history predates its data-plane job, and must not be read as data-plane uptime (2026-09-06)

`.github/workflows/supabase-keepalive.yml` now states, at the data-plane probe, that this workflow's green **15-minute tick** runs carry **no** information about the data plane. The `prod canary (auth + data plane)` job did not exist until WIC-2123 landed in `18d8a183` at 2026-09-05T22:03Z; every earlier run is green because on the 15-minute tick it ran only the auth probe, which does not dial Postgres. The `keep-alive` job **does** dial Postgres (`psql … -c 'SELECT 1;'` against the same pooler host family), but it is gated to `workflow_dispatch` and the `17 6 */3 * *` schedule, so it is **skipped** on the 15-minute ticks that make up that history. `gh run list` renders "green because healthy" and "green because unmeasured" identically.

So the workflow's transition to red at 2026-09-05T21:53Z is **this instrument landing, not a regression** — that run is the job's first execution ever, a `workflow_dispatch` on the WIC-2123 branch ten minutes before merge. Measured 2026-09-06T11:3xZ over all 50 runs: across the 9 in which the job exists it is red **9/9, from first execution**, with the data-plane **step** itself `failure` in all 9. It has never once observed a healthy data plane, so the 15-minute tick history says nothing about `/api/health`.

It is **not** silent about Postgres generally, and that distinction is worth keeping. The `keep-alive` job executed in 11 of those 50 runs and `keep-alive (production)` succeeded in all 11 — most recently 2026-09-06T10:33:20Z, in the very run whose data-plane probe failed. **psql from GitHub Actions reaches the pooler while the Worker's `/api/health` does not**, which localizes WIC-2092 to the Worker→Postgres path (Hyperdrive/egress, WIC-2097) rather than to Supabase being down. The workflow comment now carries that contrast instead of telling readers to discard the whole workflow, and warns that widening the keep-alive `if:` gate would invalidate the stated reason while leaving the sentence reading fine.

This is the same class as the `db` signature drift recorded above (WIC-2169), and the second time in two days that a green→red edge on this service was the instrument moving rather than production. Both directions of the misread are live: **do not** close or downgrade WIC-2092 by citing green canary runs from 2026-09-05 or earlier, and **do not** open a regression card for "prod broke at 21:53Z". Verify with `gh run view <id> --json jobs` — the job is absent, not passing, in every green run. Read it at **step** level (`.jobs[].steps[]`): the job-level view alone will not discriminate "absent" from "passing", and it is what shows the keep-alive's `SELECT 1` succeeding in the same run the data-plane probe fails (WIC-2175, corrected by WIC-2176 — this entry originally claimed the keep-alive does not dial Postgres and that the history was evidence in neither direction; both were false. Originally filed against WIC-2174, an unrelated card, because the id was predicted before the card was created).

Documentation only. No workflow logic, assertion or schedule changed; the probe still passes iff HTTP 200 and `.status == "ok"`.

`docs/architecture/adr/ADR-010-absent-owner-posture.md` exists to stop agents re-deriving the absent-owner burndown — its own header says so. Its **D2** row had drifted to a quarter of its stated value and, worse, presented the remainder as dispatchable work. Docs only; no code, schema, migration, baseline or guard change.

- **The drop is remediation, not a blunted guard.** The two alternative explanations were both checked and both fail: WIC-2069's guard change at `feade4d7` left the counts at 71/29 to the digit, and every baseline regeneration across the five slices was downward by deletion only. Independently, the baseline's 12 keys carry `count` fields summing to exactly the 24 findings (21 `SIG` + 3 `COND`), so no coarse key is absorbing new sites — that sum is now documented as the cheap integrity test.

D2's remainder is gated on a production data migration, not on engineering time — the signature half is done.

The header now states that each count is a measurement at a named commit, and that a re-measure must move the row and its commit together.

### Fixed — every client-side form validation message was dead: `packages/web` resolved zod 4 against `@hookform/resolvers` 3 (2026-09-05)

`PersonalInfoForm` and `ApplicationForm` never rendered a validation message. An invalid submit threw an uncaught `ZodError` and the form silently did nothing — no message, no `PATCH`, no feedback of any kind. **This supersedes the ⚠️ note in the WIC-2124 entry below, which recorded the defect as unfixed** (WIC-2126).

**The cause was one orphaned lockfile entry, not a dependency anyone chose.** `packages/web` declared `zod@^3.23.8`, but the committed lockfile carried a nested `packages/web/node_modules/zod@4.3.6` — and that entry had **no `resolved` and no `integrity` field**, the signature of a stray on-disk directory npm recorded rather than a version any dependency asked for. Nothing in the tree declares `zod@^4`: the only two declarations are `packages/api` and `packages/web`, both `^3.23.8`. Vite and node resolve from the importing file upward, so every component got zod 4 while `@hookform/resolvers@3.10.0` only understands zod 3's `ZodError`; its error guard missed and the resolver rethrew instead of populating `formState.errors`. Removing those seven lines is the whole fix — `packages/web` now resolves the hoisted `zod@3.25.76`, exactly as `packages/api` already did.

**Pinned to zod 3 rather than moving to `@hookform/resolvers` v5.** The alternative would have taken zod 4 across every schema in the package *and* split `packages/web` from `packages/api`, which is on zod 3 and unaffected. One zod over the monorepo is the smaller, more coherent tree.

**`npm ls zod` is now a CI gate** in `lint-and-test`, run straight after `npm ci`. This was a red check available the entire time and never run: the tree was invalid as committed, so `npm ls zod` exited non-zero with `ELSPROBLEMS` on a clean `npm ci`. It is scoped to `zod` deliberately — a whole-tree `npm ls --all` is red today on two unrelated pre-existing skews (`esbuild@0.19.12` against vite's `^0.27.0 || ^0.28.0`, and `@vitest/coverage-v8@1.6.1` against `vitest@4.1.11`), tracked separately; widen it once those clear.

**`noValidate` on both forms, settling the product question WIC-2124 left open.** Zod is now the single source of validation messaging. The masking was not incidental to this bug — it *was* why it survived: the URL and email inputs are `type="url"` / `type="email"`, so the browser blocked submission before React Hook Form was reached and the field merely *looked* rejected. That made a whole class of Zod failures unreachable in a browser, and therefore untestable. Checked before switching, since a `.or(z.literal(''))` union can degrade to a bare `Invalid input`: it does not — every affected field yields its specific authored message (`Must be a valid URL`, `Must be a valid email address`, `Must be a valid URL starting with http:// or https://`). `PersonalInfoForm` also picks up the accessible-error pattern `ApplicationForm` already used — `aria-invalid`, `aria-describedby` pointing at the message, `role="alert"`, and `aria-required` on the four required fields — because with the native layer off the Zod `<p>` is the only signal a user gets.

**Regression cover, which neither form had.** `PersonalInfoForm.validation.test.tsx` asserts two layers that fail independently: the `zodResolver` contract itself (the tightest detector of a version skew, no render needed) and the rendered message reaching the user. Graded against the defect by reinstalling the nested `zod@4.3.6`, it fails **3 of 6** with the exact `ZodError` rethrow; the 3 that pass are the positive controls, which are supposed to pass on both trees. The e2e assertion in `personal-info.spec.ts` is flipped from documenting the broken behaviour to asserting the message — 20/20 in that file now pass, including the two specs that previously relied on native rejection, which the layer-agnostic `expectFieldRejected` helper was written to survive.

⚠️ **A stale dev server made the fixed e2e spec fail.** `playwright.config.ts` sets `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI`, and a `vite` process left over from the WIC-2124 investigation was still serving port 5173 **out of a different checkout** — one that still had the broken nested zod. The spec ran green against the fix only after that process was killed. A local Playwright pass certifies whichever tree the listener on 5173 was started from, not the one you are sitting in; check the port before believing either a pass or a failure.



### Changed — `packages/api` runs vitest 4, `esbuild` nests under `drizzle-kit`, and the dependency-tree baseline is now EMPTY (2026-09-06)

Both rows the WIC-2132 gate had to pin are **resolved rather than waived**, so `scripts/dependency-tree-baseline.json` ships with `"exempt": []` and a bare `npm ls --all` exits **0** on its own — the one clause of WIC-2129's acceptance that did not previously hold (WIC-2137).

- **`@vitest/coverage-v8@1.6.1`** — `packages/api` moved from `vitest@^1.6.0` to `^4.1.11`, with `@vitest/coverage-v8` moved as the matched pair. The monorepo no longer runs two majors of its own test runner: both workspaces are on 4.1.11.
- **`esbuild@0.19.12`** — the root now declares `esbuild: ^0.27.0`, which satisfies both `vite@8` copies and pushes drizzle-kit's own correct `0.19.12` down into `node_modules/drizzle-kit/node_modules/esbuild`. **The card's fence said not to do this because "drizzle-kit would break"; that premise was tested, not assumed, and it does not hold** — the break it predicts is a *shared* copy being raised, and npm nests instead. Verified: drizzle-kit resolves its nested `0.19.12`, both binaries execute, and `drizzle-kit generate` still loads `drizzle.config.ts` through `esbuild-register` (which declares esbuild as a peer at `>=0.12 <1`, so 0.27.7 satisfies it).

**The migration was baselined before it started, because a non-collecting suite reports green.** Pre-migration on vitest 1.6.1: **85 files / 1651 tests**. Post-migration: **85 files / 1651 tests**, and `npm run test:coverage` exits 0 with **59 files instrumented** — one more than the 58 the old text reporter listed, so nothing silently stopped being measured.

⚠️ **The coverage percentage moved a long way and no coverage got worse: 84.93% → 70.98% statements.** `@vitest/coverage-v8@4` remaps through `ast-v8-to-istanbul` instead of v1's line-based mapper, so the same executed code is scored against a stricter, AST-accurate denominator. The ruler changed, not the tests — the file inventory is a superset and every test still passes. No threshold is configured anywhere and `test:coverage` is not run in CI, so nothing gates on the number.

**Three real breaks, all in test code, none in `src/`.** Four `vi.fn()` mocks were invoked with `new` while implemented as arrow functions; vitest 4 rejects that (`did not use 'function' or 'class'`), so they became function expressions — the other six `@anthropic-ai/sdk` mocks already used `class` and needed nothing. Separately, `packages/api` now sets `hookTimeout: 30_000`: six suites build a real PGlite database in `beforeAll`, vitest 4 enforces the 10s default on them where 1.6 did not, and **which** file trips it varies run to run (three different files across three runs, each passing in isolation) — contention, not a slow suite. Under 1.6 those same files took 13.3s and 14.3s end-to-end and passed.

`packages/web`'s `vite` was refreshed 8.0.8 → 8.2.2 inside its existing `^8.0.4` range so both workspaces resolve one vite and one rolldown; without that, `vitest@4` pulled a second rolldown into `packages/api` and the gate went red on `@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-musl`. `--selftest` gains two arms that grade against an **empty** baseline, since the other seven use a hardcoded fixture and therefore pass no matter what the shipped file says (WIC-2110).


### Changed — The `npm ls` CI gate now covers the whole dependency tree, not just `zod`; and the two rows that kept it named are NOT version skews (2026-09-06)

WIC-2126 shipped `npm ls zod` as a CI gate and deferred widening it to `npm ls --all` until "two unrelated pre-existing skews" were resolved. **Measured on a clean `npm ci` at `main` `3950ae76`: there are no skews to resolve.** Both rows are **unmet OPTIONAL peers on a package hoisted for a different consumer**, which npm reports as `invalid` (WIC-2132, carrying WIC-2129).

- `packages/web/node_modules/vite@8.0.8` declares `esbuild: "^0.27.0 || ^0.28.0"` as a peer marked `"optional": true`. npm walks up, finds the root `esbuild@0.19.12` — which is **correct** for its owner, `drizzle-kit@0.21.4` requires `^0.19.7` — and judges it against *vite's* range. All four installed esbuild copies were enumerated and each is right for its own owner. (WIC-2129 attributed the nested `0.27.7` to vite; it belongs to **tsx**, which requires `~0.27.0`.)
- `packages/web/node_modules/vitest@4.1.11` declares `@vitest/coverage-v8: "4.1.11"` the same way. The hoisted `@vitest/coverage-v8@1.6.1` belongs to `packages/api`, which declares `vitest: ^1.6.0` **and** `@vitest/coverage-v8: ^1.6.0` and resolves the hoisted 1.6.1 pair — an exact, self-consistent match.

**So WIC-2129's coverage alarm is retired as a false alarm: `packages/api`'s coverage output was never wrong, and no coverage threshold or number this repo has quoted is at risk.** `packages/api` is the only workspace with a `test:coverage` script and therefore the only consumer of coverage; `packages/web` declares no coverage package and never runs it. Migrating `packages/api` from vitest 1.6.x to vitest 4 is a real modernisation and is filed separately — it is not a prerequisite for this gate.

**A bare `npm ls --all` was rejected, not adopted.** It exits 1 on that optional-peer noise on every run, forever — trading WIC-2126's false green for a permanent false red, the same disease as WIC-2122 and WIC-2131. The two rows are instead pinned in `scripts/dependency-tree-baseline.json` **with the reason each is exempt**, shrink-only and bidirectionally: a new invalid row fails, and a baselined row that has been *resolved* also fails, so the file can only shrink. Same idiom as `A11Y_BASELINE` / `AXE_BASELINE`. `--omit=peer`, `--omit=optional` and both together were measured and suppress **neither** row (they are *unmet* peers — there is no installed peer edge to omit); `--omit=dev` exits 0 only by deleting the entire dev tree, where vitest, vite and eslint live.

**The exemption is verified on every run, not asserted once.** `scripts/dependency-tree-check.py` re-reads the requiring package's own `package.json` and confirms `peerDependenciesMeta[<name>].optional === true` for every `"<range>" from <path>` clause npm attached to the row. Keying on the package *name* would let a future genuine skew inherit an exemption written for a different reason; if vite ever makes that peer required, the entry stops applying and the build goes red with nobody having to remember to revisit it. Non-`invalid` problems (`missing:`, `extraneous:`) are never exemptible.

Graded two ways, since Code Reviewer is paused and no human review was available. `--selftest` runs eight offline fixtures — new row, resolved-and-therefore-stale row, expired exemption, unconditional problem, patch-bump-is-not-a-failure, and both path arms — and runs in CI *before* the real check, so a regression in the checker cannot present as a clean tree. And a live mutation against the real installed tree: pointing `packages/web` at `date-fns@^5.0.0` makes `npm ls --all` report a third row and the gate exits **1**, naming it and classifying it `hard_requirement`; reverted, it exits 0. ⚠️ The first mutation attempt — editing `node_modules/date-fns/package.json` — **did not apply**: npm reads installed versions from `node_modules/.package-lock.json`, so the tree was unchanged and the gate graded green on a mutant that was never there.

⚠️ **npm redacts UUID-shaped segments from every path it prints.** This fleet's checkouts live under `.../workspaces/<agent-uuid>/...`, so `npm ls` reports install paths as `.../workspaces/***/wt-.../node_modules/esbuild` — a path that exists nowhere and that `Path.relative_to()` rejects, silently leaving an absolute redacted path in the baseline that then matches nothing. A CI runner's path has no UUID and never triggers it, so the failure is invisible where the check *runs* and only bites where the baseline is *authored*. `relativize()` falls back to the longest trailing run of segments that actually exists under the repo root — longest, because a shortest match would collapse `packages/web/node_modules/zod` onto a hoisted `node_modules/zod` and silently merge two distinct rows.



### Fixed — the workflow checklist read "0 of 0 steps completed" on every cold page load (2026-09-06)

Giving the fourth checklist row a tri-state (the entry below, WIC-2141) made a state reachable that never was before: all four rows unknown at once. `totalCount = items.length - unknownCount` is then `4 - 4 = 0`, and the header read **"0 of 0 steps completed"** above **"Checking 4 more steps…"**. That is the *common* path, not an edge case — `ApplicationDetail` fires all four artefact queries on mount and renders the checklist as soon as the *application* query resolves, so every cold load passes through it (WIC-2153, carrying WIC-2150).

- **Nothing was broken; it just read as nonsense, twice in one card.** The `totalCount === 0` guard held, so no NaN, and the percentage correctly withheld to "—". But the count line states a settled figure over an empty denominator, and "**more** steps" has no referent when there are no known steps to be more than. Both are fixed: the count line is withheld entirely at a zero denominator, and the word "more" drops with it — "Checking 4 steps…".
- **Withheld rather than reworded.** The count line's job is to report progress against known steps; with none known there is no progress to report, and any wording of a zero denominator invites the reader to treat "0 of 0" as a real ratio. The `Checking N steps…` line carries the whole signal in that window and is already the honest one.
- **The comment above the count line said the denominator's floor was 1.** True until WIC-2141, false after it. It now records that the floor is 0, that the *rendered* denominator therefore floors at 1, and why "steps" stays literal at 1 — the same standing-comment failure WIC-2141 was itself filed for, one card later and in the same component.
