Which side your entry is on depends on which merge you are looking at, and every entry goes through two that point opposite ways — the pre-push `git merge <base>` on your branch (your head is `ours`, so your **trailing** edge is at the join) and the landing merge where the base takes your PR (your head is `theirs`, so your **leading** edge is). The tie-break named the pre-push edge, while the landing merge is the one that publishes a weld to `main`. Documentation only; no code, no behaviour change (WIC-1802, routed as WIC-1815).

- **Verified by running one pair of inputs both directions.** PRs #188 (`fcc5e4e`) and #180 (`c6cf108`), siblings on `fix/wic1478-…` (`a18981e`), `main` at `a46c63a`: when `main` merges #180 in, the weld lands on #180's heading with its leading blank consumed; when #180's branch merges that same `main` in, the weld lands on #188's heading and the blank that went is #180's trailing one. Same two files, opposite direction, opposite edge. So the guidance is now "pad both edges" with the tie-break retired, rather than a preference between them. Both branch tips are weld-free at those heads — this is a measurement of what the merges will do, not a defect owed by either author.
- **For two PRs stacked on the same base, no per-branch arrangement is safe in both merge orders.** Their entries become adjacent on `main`, so the contested join is between the two siblings and the edge needing padding belongs to whichever merges second — which neither author controls. Measured across ten variant refs, all individually weld-free, each merged for real in a scratch worktree: every single-edge remedy is clean in exactly one of the two orders and welds in the other.
- **The row that changes the advice: padding both edges of _both_ siblings welds in both orders, exactly as badly as padding neither.** Padding both edges of exactly one sibling is clean in both. So the obvious move — every author applies the documented remedy to their own branch — is precisely the arrangement that fails, and the remedy cannot be reasoned about one branch at a time. A blank added at an uncontested seam changes how diff3 aligns the contested one: with a leading blank on both siblings the merged file carries a stray double blank above the first entry and still welds at the join below it.
- **So the merge-result check gets a named owner rather than a better prevention.** Whoever merges the second of two siblings runs it in that merge commit before pushing — the first moment the two blocks are adjacent, and the last before the weld enters a merge base other branches inherit. Both branch tips report clean and neither PR page shows it; nothing in CI runs it today (WIC-1792).

### Fixed — the changelog rule told you to pad the wrong end of your entry, and the weld is now the only defect queued to land (2026-08-30)

Root `CLAUDE.md` named the welded-heading union artifact as one failure mode of three and left it at that — no prevention, and no sense of how often it fires. Simulating all 74 open PRs whose `CHANGELOG.md` differs from their true base, with the three-input control, puts it at **9 PRs welding a `### ` heading and 0 introducing a duplicate bullet or heading**. It is not one of three; it is currently the whole queue. New `CLAUDE.md` subsection states the prevention and the measurement (WIC-1567 follow-up).

- **The prevention is one blank line, and it goes above your entry, not below.** Rebuilding each of the nine branches with an extra blank added to every inserted run and re-running the simulation: as-is **9** welds, extra **leading** blank **0**, extra **trailing** blank **9** — no effect at all. The instinct to pad the end of what you wrote is exactly wrong, because the blank the driver consumes is the one above your heading. A leading blank without keeping the trailing one just moves the weld onto the next entry's heading, so the rule is both.
- **All nine branch files are individually clean, and so is `main`.** The defect exists only in the merge result, so no PR page shows it and no post-merge check on `main` predicts it. This is the concrete argument for the pre-push simulation over a clean `git merge`, which the union driver will happily report as success.
- **Sharing an anchor does not imply welding, so the tally cannot stand in for the simulation.** Resolved to content anchors the nine do all sit on a shared seam, and on only three of them — five before `### Docs — Two heading rulings…`, two before `### Fixed — Every match and gap row…`, two before `### Added — restoreFocusTo…`. But the most contended anchor in the file, eight PRs stacked at the top of `[Unreleased]`, welds zero times. The anchor command answers whether GitHub will call a PR CONFLICTING; only the union simulation answers whether the driver will corrupt the result.
- **The anchor command itself was tallying incomparable numbers, and is replaced.** It grouped raw `@@ -N` hunk positions, but each N is in that PR's _own_ merge base's coordinates and the 49 open `main`-based PRs sit on **22 distinct merge bases** — so it split one real anchor across several N and merged unrelated anchors sharing an N. Both errors were live: the eight PRs at the top anchor span five merge bases, and #242 at `@@ -63` and #211 at `@@ -116` are the same seam. Only top-of-`[Unreleased]` was exempt, because the backfill note has pinned it to line ~10 since `1ea6186` — which is precisely why the broken tally looked trustworthy, its largest bucket being the one position it could not get wrong. The replacement resolves each hunk to the `### ` heading it lands in front of and tallies that.
- **Found by tripping over it.** The first draft of this entry picked its slot off the old tally, and the conflict-delta check caught that the slot was already #242's seam. The entry moved, and "a clear anchor is necessary but not sufficient — measure the conflict delta before pushing" is now written down next to the command that misled its own author.
- **No branch is accused and no card is filed.** The nine are named as a measurement at a head, not as a defect owed by their authors: each resolves the moment its author adopts the leading-blank convention, and the merge result is the thing at fault. All nine were re-measured at their current heads immediately before this shipped, and all nine still weld.
- **This entry follows its own rule** — inserted with a leading blank line, before a heading measured to carry no other open PR's hunk, and re-checked for conflict delta across all 49 open `main`-based PRs.

### Fixed — a code span in the WIC-1377 entry never rendered, and a formatter run over it silently ate five spaces (2026-08-30)

That entry quotes a Drizzle raw template, and wrote it as a single-backtick code span with the two inner backticks backslash-escaped. CommonMark does not honour a backslash escape inside a code span: the escape is ignored for delimiter scanning, the span closes at the first inner backtick, and every code span in the rest of the paragraph inverts. Parsed as CommonMark, **all 8** of that paragraph's code spans held prose while the SQL and route fragments rendered as plain text, and its `**parameter list**` reached the page as literal asterisks. It has been rendering that way since it landed on 2026-08-26, on the repository's own front page, with no gate in this repo able to see it. Rewritten in the padded double-backtick form, which needs no escape; with backticks, backslashes and spaces stripped the two versions are byte-identical, so nothing but the delimiters moved (WIC-1732, found during the WIC-1613 review on PR #221).

- **Prettier was the messenger, not the bug.** Reported as a Prettier defect — five word-boundary spaces lost in an untouched paragraph, leaving prose that reads "a sql-backtick-span template" with no space at the seam, at exit code 0 — but Prettier is faithfully re-serialising the inverted tree above, and a code span requires no surrounding whitespace, so the spaces have nowhere to be. That reframes the fix: exempting the paragraph with `<!-- prettier-ignore -->` would have frozen a paragraph that was already wrong. Classified over the whole file at Prettier 3.8.3, `--parser markdown`: **63** lines of `*em*` → `_em_` churn, **10** blank lines removed, and **exactly 1** destructive change — this one. After the fix that class is **0**, and the paragraph round-trips with zero diff on its own.
- **The format glob must not be widened to reach this file, and the reason is not churn.** Measured at `main` = `e3533d7`, every one of the **10** blank lines Prettier removes sits immediately above a `### ` heading — eight entry seams — which is precisely the leading pad the union-driver weld remedy prescribes. Prettier collapses a run of blank lines to one and cannot tell a separator from a pad, so pointing the formatter at `CHANGELOG.md` would strip the remedy from eight entries in a single commit and re-arm the weld on each. The two conventions are in direct conflict and the padding wins; `format:check` staying scoped to `packages/**` is load-bearing, not an oversight. Recorded in root `CLAUDE.md` beside the padding rule, together with the authoring rule that produced this entry.
- **The class is invisible in the source and only shows up in the parsed output.** Nothing in the raw markdown looks wrong, the escapes read as careful rather than broken, and both the review of PR #221 and the card that filed this read the damage as reflow rather than as a mis-parse that predated it. The check that catches it is to render the paragraph and count the code spans; this entry was written that way, and the first draft of the `CLAUDE.md` prose describing the bug reproduced it and was caught by exactly that step.

### Docs — the claim that GitHub ignores the changelog union driver is withdrawn as unreproducible (2026-08-30)

`CLAUDE.md` told readers that GitHub computes mergeability without consulting `.gitattributes`, so a `CHANGELOG.md` that `merge=union` had resolved locally would still sit `CONFLICTING / DIRTY` on the PR page. That claim is withdrawn. It is not reproducible at `main` `78abadf`: of the 48 open `MERGEABLE` PRs that touch `CHANGELOG.md`, 34 genuinely diverge from their base on that file, and **none of the 34 collide with the driver switched off**. A PR whose changelog merges only because of union — the one shape that could tell the two theories apart — does not exist in the queue today, so the section now records that the question is open rather than asserting an answer. The practical instruction is unchanged and now rests on a measurement rather than on the withdrawn premise: leave `merge=union` in place, and do not migrate to changelog fragments on the strength of a claim in either direction (supersedes the WIC-1543 entry below).

- **The conflict backlog on this file is zero, and the PR flag does not show it.** GitHub currently calls 29 PRs `CONFLICTING`. Exactly three have a genuine conflict, and not one of the three is on `CHANGELOG.md` — #160 on `ApplicationsList.tsx`, #154 and #147 on `deploy.yml` and `docs/analytics/`. For the other 26, GitHub has itself computed a two-parent merge commit at `refs/pull/N/merge` carrying zero conflict markers. Certify from that merge ref or from a real `git merge`; the `mergeable` field alone is an upper bound that decays.
- **Replay a PR against the base its merge ref was built on, not against the current tip.** All 26 of those merge refs name an _older_ `main` as their first parent. Replaying each head against current `main` reports all 26 as "would conflict without union"; replaying against `merge-base(p1, head)` reports **0 of 22**. Same PRs, same driver, opposite conclusion — the first figure is an artifact of a base that moved underneath the measurement, and it is the same coordinate-system error the weld check and the anchor tally were each corrected for earlier.
- **`git merge-file` was mislabelled as "what GitHub sees".** It ignores `.gitattributes`, so it answers a real and useful question — what the merge does with the driver off — but that is not a reproduction of GitHub's view, and calling it one is what made the withdrawn claim look verified. `git merge-tree` is worse for this purpose: it reads merge attributes from the _working tree_ unless `--attr-source` is passed to `git` itself, before the subcommand.

### Fixed — the command palette opened as a dialog with no accessible name at all (2026-08-30)

- `CommandPalette`'s `Dialog.Content` rendered with neither a `Dialog.Title` nor a `Dialog.Description`, so a screen reader announced "dialog" and stopped. Not a bad name — **no** name, on the surface a keyboard-first user reaches most often (WCAG 2.1 AA, SC 4.1.2). Radix had been saying so in the console on every single mount.
- Both are `sr-only`. The palette's design is that it opens with nothing above the search field, so the fix has to add a name without adding a heading.
- **Neither may take an `id` prop, and that is load-bearing rather than style.** Radix's `TitleWarning` / `DescriptionWarning` resolve `context.titleId` / `context.descriptionId` through `getElementById` (`@radix-ui/react-dialog` 1.1.15, `dist/index.mjs:295` and `:308`), so an overridden id leaves that lookup empty and **the warning fires against markup that is correct** — which is how a real warning gets trained into background noise. `ApplicationForm.tsx:227` overrides it and warns today for exactly that reason; its dialog is genuinely named and described.
- The footer's `↑↓` and `↵` were announced by Unicode name, and `↵` is "downwards arrow with corner leftwards" — not a key anyone can go and press. Each glyph is now `aria-hidden` with the key's spoken name beside it, the same hidden-plus-`sr-only` shape WIC-1850 used on the result rows. The third `<kbd>` in that footer, `ESC`, is deliberately left alone: it already spells its key, and a blanket sweep over every `<kbd>` would have given it a redundant label.
- Reusing the footer as the description via `aria-describedby`, rather than writing a second copy of the instructions, was tried and rejected — that copy is written to be glanced at and reads as a stutter aloud ("Navigate with arrow keys, up and down arrow keys to navigate…"), and it says nothing about typing. Both rulings are recorded in `docs/design/ACCESSIBILITY.md`, under a new "Dialogs" subsection and as a third row on the existing glyph rule.
- Six new tests in `CommandPalette.test.tsx`; **four fail without the component change** and the two that do not are controls. One asserts no Radix warning fires, and it carries a positive control that mounts a deliberately unnamed dialog — without it the guard would pass just as happily against a broken spy or a Radix version that had stopped warning.

### Fixed — the changelog checks swept the wrong merge orientation, and the blank-line remedy was backwards (2026-08-30)

Every union simulation this file has shipped put the PR head on the `theirs` side, which models the PR merging into its base. That is not the operation anyone performs here: a `CONFLICTING` PR becomes mergeable by running `git merge <base>` _on the PR branch_, and `git merge` puts the current branch on `ours`. Side order is not cosmetic — union concatenates ours-then-theirs inside each differing region, so it decides both where a duplicated bullet lands and which side loses its separator blank. Corrected in `CLAUDE.md`, with the consequences below (WIC-1778, from QA's WIC-1772; the orientation error was theirs to find, not mine).

- **The orientation is settled by measurement, not argument.** PR #115 was merged for real in a scratch worktree and the result compared byte-for-byte against both simulations: `ours = PR head` is **byte-identical** to what `git merge` wrote, and `ours = base branch` differs, first at line 598.
- **The wrong orientation loses hits silently, and it is a strict subset.** Across the 81 open PRs — 78 with a `CHANGELOG.md` differing from their true base, `main` at `ee6c217` — the real orientation finds **1 misfiled bullet and 11 welding PRs**; the old one finds **0 and 10**. It surfaced nothing the corrected sweep missed, and missed a live defect in each row. The previously published "the misfiling check returns zero across the board" was an artifact of side order, not a clean board.
- **The blank-line prevention was published back to front.** The block that loses its separator is the one union emits _second_; with your PR head on `ours` your block is emitted **first**, so the blank consumed is the one at its **end**. Re-tested over all 11 welders: as-is **11**, extra leading blank **11 — no effect**, extra trailing blank **1**, both **1**. Confirmed against a real merge, not only a simulation: PR #92 rebuilt each way and actually merged still welds with a leading blank and does not weld with a trailing one. The earlier entry above, which told readers the leading blank was the fix and that padding the end "does nothing", is superseded on that point — its reasoning was sound for the orientation it measured.
- **One welder resists the remedy.** #149 still welds with a trailing blank and with both, so blank-line discipline is a strong default rather than a guarantee, and the simulation remains the thing that answers the question for a given branch.
- **Two checks now ship together, because one corruption has two presentations.** A bullet that union both duplicates and relocates reads as _misfiled_ when the copy lands under a foreign heading and as a _same-heading duplicate_ when both land under one — and which you get flips with side order. On WIC-1768's own fixture the same three files give 0 misfiled / 1 duplicate in the real orientation and 2 / 0 in the old one, so the misfiling check alone would have called that PR clean in the orientation that matters. Neither check is a superset of the other; both are threshold-free.
- **The self-heal test has a stated exception now.** "Present in the merge base ⇒ passenger, files nothing" holds only while the deletion stays one-sided. When the branch also edits that region the merge driver is consulted after all and concatenates instead of deleting, so the superseded text survives a merge the test predicts will remove it. PR #115 is the counterexample, and for a stacked PR the correction may live on its base branch rather than `main`.

### Fixed — a committed changelog weld is not cosmetic; it arms a misfile for every branch stacked on you (2026-08-30)

`CLAUDE.md` has treated the welded `### ` heading — a heading left sitting directly against the previous entry's last bullet — as a legibility defect with a one-blank-line prevention, and reassured readers that the nine welding PRs would "self-resolve once each author adopts the convention". Both halves are wrong, and the second is the expensive one. A welded heading sits _inside_ the previous bullet's diff3 region, so the next ordinary edit to that bullet drags the heading with it and union files the edited copy under whatever entry it lands after. The weld corrupts nothing itself; it converts the next routine change into a misfiling (WIC-1567).

- **Observed end to end on live branches, four steps in two hours.** A routine `merge origin/main` on `fix/wic1478-dashboard-attention-aggregates` welded a heading and the weld was **committed** in the merge commit (07:25Z; every earlier commit on that branch carries zero welds). That commit became the merge base shared with two stacked PRs, #188 and #180. At 09:33Z the parent extended the welded bullet by one line — and both children's merges now file the **corrected** copy under a foreign heading while the superseded copy keeps the right home, under two _different_ foreign headings, which is itself proof the merge invented the placement rather than inheriting it.
- **The repair window closes when the weld reaches a shared merge base.** Same three inputs with only the welds removed: as-is both children misfile; the weld repaired _today_ on the parent, both still misfile; the weld never committed, both clean. Repairing afterwards is just another edit in the contested region and cannot reach the base the children branched from. #188's author had already repaired the weld on their own branch an hour earlier and it bought them nothing — downstream repair does not protect you.
- **The blank line is a prevention, not a repair.** Run the check after _every_ `merge main` that touches this file, not only before a push, and fix it in that same commit. Caught before commit it costs one blank line; caught two hours later it cost two PRs.
- **The published weld roster was stale on arrival, and this file now says why.** The previous entry named eleven PRs including #211 and #248; both had been repaired at 08:13Z and 08:16Z, _before_ that PR was opened at 08:19Z and long before it merged at 09:29Z. The re-measure rule exists precisely to catch this and it did not, because the accused set had grown from one branch to eleven and re-checking eleven by hand quietly gets skipped. Every accused PR is now quoted at a head SHA, and the instruction is to re-run the one sweep rather than spot-check. Re-run immediately before this entry merged rather than quoted from the draft: **9 welders across 86 open PRs** at `30b61a2`, #92 #93 #118 #123 #149 #165 #171 #179 #208 — the population had grown by three while the entry was written, the roster and every head SHA had not.

### Fixed — onboarding's terminal "Create Application Now" button created nothing (2026-08-29)

The last thing a new user is asked to do on the first-run flow was a no-op. Step 5's primary-styled CTA ran `handleCompleteStep(5)` behind a `// This would open the application form modal` comment: it advanced the wizard and created no application, with no error, toast, or explanation. At the UI level the failure was indistinguishable from success, and it silently falsified the step's own promise that "you can create your first application now".

- **The CTA now navigates to the real create form at `/applications/new`** rather than opening a form inside the onboarding dialog. That route already exists in `App.tsx` and is what the Dashboard's own "Add Application" link uses, so this needs no new UI — which also keeps the fix clear of the in-dialog focus-trap problem (`MODAL_FOCUS_MANAGEMENT_SPEC.md` §2) that made the "render a form in the modal" option expensive.
- **It routes through the existing `handleFinishAndGo`, not a bare `navigate`.** Reaching step 5 only advances local state, so leaving without completing first means the provider re-fetches an untouched status and reopens the modal on top of the form the user was just sent to. This is the same hazard, and the same helper, as the step 6 shortcuts (WIC-1032).
- **The redundant "I'll Do This Later" button is removed.** Its handler was identical to the footer's "Next Step", so the step rendered three controls with two behaviours. The footer remains the way to decline. This matches the rule step 6 already follows: every visible control does something different.
- **Reversal-checked.** Three of the four new step-5 tests fail against the unfixed component. The two `it.todo`s parked on PR #82 are also written out, since that PR has landed and the helper they were waiting for is now what step 5 depends on.
- **`ONBOARDING_FLOW.md` is corrected in the same change.** It documented the CTA as "Opens ApplicationForm modal" — a behaviour the build never had — so the doc would have certified the defect as intended design.

### CI — the no-deploy merge marker is now `[skip deploy]`; `[skip ci]` no longer silently hides the docs audits (2026-08-30)

`[skip ci]` was doing two unrelated jobs: "don't deploy" and, as a GitHub-native directive, "suppress the entire workflow run". The second job also suppressed the five audits in `Lint & Test` — three of which (`doc-reference-audit`, `route-title-table-audit`, `wireframe-casing-audit`) gate **only** `docs/`. So a docs commit was both the only change that could break those audits and exactly the change `[skip ci]` waved through. Measured on `main` 2026-08-30: of 18 `[skip ci]` commits touching `docs/`, 13 were direct pushes that never ran the audits; `f07b9f6` landed a dangling ADR citation that way and sat red ~2.5h, failing every branch rebased onto it (WIC-1877, routed from WIC-1874).

- **`[skip deploy]` is the no-deploy route now** (`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`). It is not a GitHub directive, so the run still fires and `Lint & Test` always runs on `main`; the `deploy-production` `if:` reads `github.event.head_commit.message` and skips only the deploy. `workflow_dispatch` (the manual production lever) is never skip-gated.
- **`E2E Tests` is also gated on `[skip deploy]` for pushes** — a no-deploy merge's runtime behaviour was already covered by the PR's own E2E run and no deploy follows, so re-running Playwright on the merge commit is pure duplication. It still runs on every `pull_request` and `workflow_dispatch`.
- **`[skip deploy]` is complementary to, not a replacement for, the two skip-CI controls that already landed.** WIC-2094 removed the fail-open `docs/` predicate from the skip-CI allowlist (`.github/scripts/runtime-paths.cjs`), so a `[skip ci]` PR that edits a `docs/design/*.py` gate script is now blocked while `.md` prose and `.github/workflows/**` stay on the deliberate no-deploy `[skip ci]` route; WIC-1867 added the hourly scheduled `main` docs audit (`docs-audit.yml`) as the backstop. `[skip deploy]` adds immediacy — the run fires at merge/push time, so the audits validate the change then rather than after the fact. This change does **not** alter `skip-ci-guard.yml` / `skip-ci-sweeper.yml`.
- **Documented** in `CI_CD.md`.

### Fixed — merging an older duplicate walked a company's first-seen date forward (2026-08-26)

`mergeCompanies` reconciled `applicationCount` and `aliases` when folding duplicates together but never wrote `firstSeenAt`, so the survivor kept its own date unconditionally. Found by QA while writing the first tests for the UC-2 dedup endpoints (WIC-1360, from WIC-1354).

- **The common case is the wrong one.** Duplicates appear because a company was re-entered under a new spelling, which makes the _source_ the older row — so the typical merge moved `firstSeen` forward. `firstSeen` is what the catalog reports as the start of a company relationship, so any tenure or recency reading was wrong for exactly the companies that had been deduped, i.e. dedup degraded the one field it should have improved.
- **The loss was silent and unreachable through the API.** The source is soft-deleted, `listCompanies` filters deleted rows by default, and `toCompanyDTO` surfaces `firstSeen` from the survivor alone. The earlier date survived only in the soft-deleted row in the database, which is why this is a correctness bug rather than data destruction.
- **The survivor now takes the minimum across the target and every source.** An empty source read leaves the target's own date in place, and the merge can now only move `firstSeen` backwards or leave it — never forwards.
- **The sibling tag merges were checked and are not affected.** `mergeJobFitTags` and `mergeTechStackTags` are the same code shape and hard-delete their duplicates, so the equivalent bug would be unrecoverable — but neither `toJobFitTagDTO` nor `toTechStackTagDTO` exposes a date at all, and the tables' only date columns are `createdAt`/`updatedAt`, which carry no first-sighting meaning. Nothing to reconcile.
- **The two WIC-1354 gap tests are replaced by three that pin the rule in both directions.** The `it.fails` retention test loses its `.fails`; the gap sentinel asserting the payload has _no_ `firstSeenAt` key is retired, since it now describes the bug rather than the contract. In its place: the target's own date is kept when every source is newer — which an unconditional `firstSeenAt: sources[0].firstSeenAt` would fail while still passing the retention test — and the minimum is taken across _all_ sources, not just the first. All three assert the payload handed to the transaction, so they track the real code path; reverting the one-line `.set` change fails exactly those 3. Removal is the weakest mutation available, though, so the reconciliation was also _weakened_ three ways rather than only deleted: `sources[0].firstSeenAt` unconditionally fails 2, flipping the comparison to a maximum fails 3, and dropping the `target.firstSeenAt` seed from the `reduce` fails 1. Every variant is caught, so the three tests pin the rule itself and not merely the presence of the key.

### Fixed — the catalog and STAR bullet services no longer fall open when a request carries no owner (2026-08-29)

The AC-T0 guard (WIC-1600, ADR-010) was baselined at `origin/main` `1c54133`. Merging `5e2956b` a day later failed it on **19 new owner-absent branches** — every one of them added by a commit that was itself a tenancy fix (WIC-1365, WIC-1373, WIC-1377, WIC-1395, WIC-1360, WIC-1449, WIC-1465). Each fix scoped the row it was fixing and wrote the fallback back in on the way past (WIC-1638).

- **The owner is now required, not optional.** Eleven entry points moved from `userId?: string` to `userId: string`: the three catalog merges, the two tag updates, `generateDiff`, and the five resume-variant / interview-prep entry points that read the STAR bullet catalog. Every predicate that read `userId ? and(id, owner) : eq(id)` is now an unconditional `and(id, owner)`, so an owner-less merge can no longer select, fold, soft-delete or hard-delete across tenants.
- **`bulletOwnerScope` was the one that mattered most.** It was added to *both* `resume-variant.service.ts` and `interviewPrep.service.ts` specifically to centralise owner scoping, and it was written with the fallback baked into its signature — so centralising the shape multiplied it by every future call site rather than fixing it. Its `isNull(quantifiedBullets.userId)` fallback was genuinely fail-closed post-`0017` (NULLs rewritten to the sentinel, then `SET NOT NULL`), but it kept an absent owner *representable*, which is the defect. **The helper itself is now gone, and not because of this change:** WIC-1601 landed on `main` first and replaced it with a generic `ownerScope(table, userId?)` shared across `resume_variants`, `resumes`, `applications`, `interview_preps` and `tech_stack_tags`. That helper keeps the `isNull` fallback and has to — those first four columns are nullable, their insert paths write `userId ?? null`, and ten entry points across the two files still take `userId?: string`, so requiring the owner there would break the ADR-003 local-dev anonymous path rather than harden it. The required-owner guarantee for the STAR catalog is therefore carried by `requireOwner` at the route edge and by `userId: string` on the five entry points that reach it, which makes the fallback unreachable from those paths and leaves it fail-closed on `quantified_bullets` regardless (`.notNull()` since `0017`). Reconciled in WIC-1764 when this branch merged `main`; the two services' `ownerScope` doc comments carry the standing warning not to "finish the job" by making `userId` required. This is not a judgement call made at the merge: ADR-010's WIC-1756 correction, on this branch's own base, independently measured the same change on `origin/main` `614ad91` (resume-variant 17 -> 10, interviewPrep 15 -> 9) and records the replacement helper as **fail-closed** across the 27 sites it now serves, noting that the fail-closed shape is the majority shape in these two files.
- **Absence is rejected at the route edge for the eleven entry points in scope here — not tree-wide.** The routes laundered a null owner into an optional argument with `c.get('userId') ?? undefined`, pushing the decision down into every predicate. A new `requireOwner(c)` raises `401 OWNER_REQUIRED` at those eleven instead, which is where the `sub`-less-JWT caller from WIC-1554 — a token that verifies but resolves to `userId: null` — now stops. The empty string is rejected explicitly, since `''` is representable on `HonoVariables.userId` and is falsy in exactly the way the old ternary was. **The same laundering remains everywhere else**: measured at `8d386de`, 21 other `c.get('userId') ?? undefined` call sites survive in these same three route files (catalog 11, interview-preps 6, resume-variants 4) and 42 more elsewhere in `packages/api/src`, tracked by WIC-1549 / WIC-1554 / WIC-1596 / WIC-1435. Read those figures as a dated measurement, not a standing claim — the same shape appears **74** times on the base branch `2f18c34`, because the eleven sites this PR converts are still laundered there.
- **This does not pre-empt ADR-010 D3.** Whether local dev without Supabase config should resolve a real `LOCAL_DEV_USER_ID` instead of an absence is still open with the board. Until it lands, an owner-less request to these routes is a `401` rather than a silent cross-tenant read — the intended posture, not a regression. The three route suites that relied on the auth bypass now supply a real caller via `test/helpers/authed-app.ts`.
- **The baseline was regenerated downward, never appended.** 157 -> **131** findings across the same 30 shape-keys: all 19 new sites retired plus 7 pre-existing ones in the same files, and no key rose. Per-key, every delta in the WIC-1638 table is matched or exceeded.
- **Merging `main` moved it again, to 122 across 29 keys — and two keys did rise (WIC-1764).** WIC-1601's generic `ownerScope` replaced eleven conditional owner-absent branches with unconditional calls, so the `COND` keys fell 6 -> 1 in `interviewPrep.service.ts`, 6 -> 1 in `resume-variant.service.ts`, and 1 -> 0 for the remaining `if` test, retiring that key entirely. Against that, each file's `SIG` key rose by exactly one — 6 -> 7 and 4 -> 5 — and in both cases the riser *is* the generic helper itself, whose `userId` must stay optional for the nullable tables it now also serves. Eleven branches traded for two signatures on one centralising predicate, net **-9** sites. The baseline was re-accepted deliberately with `--write-baseline`, which is the case that flag documents; **the earlier "no key rose" claim is true only of the pre-merge tree and is superseded here.** **Do not read the -9 as a posture improvement.** Part of it is real and part is consolidation — collapsing two helpers into one retires findings without changing any caller's behaviour — and ADR-010 is explicit that this number is *the count of owner-absent branches*, never a safety score. The tree-wide absent-owner posture is still open and is finished by WIC-1549 / WIC-1554 / WIC-1596 / WIC-1435, not by anything in this merge.
- **22 new tests assert that an owner-less request reads and writes nothing.** A not-found guard and an ownership guard return the same status, so the route tests assert `not.toHaveBeenCalled()` on the service rather than a response code — proving the request stopped at the edge instead of reaching a query that merely matched no rows. A second pass over the same table pins AC-5, that a caller *with* an owner still reaches the service with its `sub`. The service-level tests keep asserting rendered SQL (the WIC-1377 precedent) and smuggle `undefined` past the type to pin the predicate itself, rather than trusting the compiler to prove the path unreachable. After the WIC-1601 reconciliation above, the two owner-less STAR cases assert that the surviving term is `"quantified_bullets"."user_id" is null` — the generic helper's absent-owner form, which selects the empty set on a `.notNull()` column — instead of the equality the retired `bulletOwnerScope` emitted. Both are fail-closed; only the shape changed. The `bulletOwnerScope`-fallback mutant retired with the helper, so the bite check is now two mutants: fail-open `requireOwner` kills 11 and restoring the `mergeCompanies` ternary kills 2, each at its predicted count. Re-measured after the merge, a third mutant covers the replacement — making the generic `ownerScope` fail open on the absent branch (`sql\`true\`` in place of `isNull`) kills **11**, including both rewritten cases and nine of WIC-1601's own, at 757 tests collected either way.

### Added — the AC-T0 guard now catches writes that ignore the owner entirely, not only ones that branch on its absence (2026-08-29)

The guard's `[SIG]` and `[COND]` checks measure *fail-open owner predicates*. A write that never mentions the owner at all satisfies the letter of both, so it produced no finding and appeared in **neither the numerator nor the denominator** of the 157 → 131 burndown — its absence read as health. Found by QA auditing PR #220 (WIC-1672, from WIC-1600 / ADR-010 D5).

- **The missed class is strictly worse than the one being burned down.** A fail-open ternary degrades only when the owner is absent; a write with no owner term fires unconditionally, **even when the owner is present**, matching every tenant's row. The owner was in scope at all six sites QA found and merely unused — required at the route edge by `requireOwner`, threaded through four frames, then dropped at the write.
- **`[NOWNER]` keys on the schema column, not on a parameter name.** Owner-bearing tables are read out of `packages/api/src/db/schema.ts` at run time, so a new table with a `user_id` column is in scope the day it lands — and unlike the name-based checks it cannot be evaded by renaming `userId` to `callerId` or hiding optionality behind a type alias, the two one-line re-spellings QA demonstrated.
- **It gates on cardinality, because the severities differ.** Of 46 UPDATE/DELETE sites against the 21 owner-bearing tables: 21 owner-scoped, 18 scoped by a primary key or `.unique()` column (at most one row, so not cross-tenant by cardinality — counted, not gated), 0 unresolvable, and **7 scoped by a non-unique key with no owner term**. Only the last class fails.
- **Three of the 7 were previously unreported.** `project.service.ts:464`, `:512` and `:548` are all `db.update(projects).set({ updatedAt }).where(eq(projects.slug, slug))`, and `projects` declares `uniqueIndex('idx_projects_user_slug').on(t.userId, t.slug)` — so `slug` alone is non-unique across tenants by declaration and each touches every tenant's project with that slug. The other four are the `extraction.service.ts` catalog updates already fixed on PR #141 (WIC-1404), which is waiting on review.
- **A green run now prints what it does not assert.** The unique/pk-scoped writes, unresolvable predicates and un-gated read-side (`SELECT`) leaks are counted on every run and listed by `--stats`. A guard that prints only its own findings makes its blind spots invisible, which is how green came to be read as tree-wide owner-scoping health.
- **The guard has 21 positive controls of its own.** It is what is advertised to hold the line as *new* sites appear, and a new site has no tests yet — so its detection is now the thing under test, against a synthetic fixture tree via `--root` so the cases stay stable as the burndown proceeds. The suite pins the fail-**closed** exemption in particular: `if (!userId) throw` is the posture ADR-010 asks for, and counting it as a violation would make the fix read as the defect. That exemption is why hardening `[COND]`/`[SIG]` left `[SIG]`+`[COND]` at exactly 131 — the 13 negation-form hits it newly reaches are all early-exit guards. Baseline 131 → 138, the 7 `[NOWNER]` sites and nothing else.

### Fixed — the README front door still sent developers to a Hyperdrive binding production does not have (2026-08-29)

`README.md`, `packages/api/README.md` and `.dev.vars.example` all described production as reaching Postgres through Cloudflare Hyperdrive, and told the reader `DATABASE_URL` is "**not** used by the Worker". Both statements are false, and the second one breaks local Worker dev outright. This is the same error PR #138 corrected in the two `CLAUDE.md` files and PR #156 corrected in `API_CONTRACTS.md` — the READMEs were simply never swept, so the repo's most-read entry point stayed wrong after the authoritative docs were fixed (WIC-1660).

- **The binding has been preview-only since 2026-05-06.** `wrangler.jsonc` declares `hyperdrive` under `env.preview` alone; `git` dates the move to `4d379b8`. `db/client.ts` resolves `HYPERDRIVE` → `DATABASE_URL` → Node singleton, so production takes the second path — the Supabase transaction pooler on port 6543, via a `DATABASE_URL` Worker secret `deploy.yml` pushes.
- **The `.dev.vars.example` advice was actively harmful.** It carried `DATABASE_URL` commented out with a note that Hyperdrive handles Postgres. `npm run dev:worker` is a bare `wrangler dev` with **no `--env`**, so it loads the top-level config and gets no `HYPERDRIVE` — following the file as written yields a Worker with no database behind it, which `/health` reports as `{"hyperdrive":false,"db":"not_applicable"}`. A `200 {"status":"ok"}` on that payload is exactly the false-green WIC-1580 hardened `classify_health()` against, so the misconfiguration does not announce itself. The variable is now uncommented and set, with the reasoning inline.
- **Two historical entries repeated the claim and are corrected in place.** The 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-12 RLS entries each said the Worker reaches Postgres "as the `postgres` owner role (via Hyperdrive)". Both postdate the binding move, so both were wrong when written. Each keeps its original text with a dated correction note appended — the owner-role conclusion that carries the security argument is unchanged, only the connection path. Found by the standing duplicate-bullet sweep, which flagged the two as a matched pair.
- **Two more PR #142 corrections had never reached `packages/api/README.md`.** Its bindings table omitted `ASSETS` — the same omission that entry records fixing in the `CLAUDE.md` files — and its Environment section still asserted the Worker uses bindings "not `process.env`". That is the half-truth already retired elsewhere: `nodejs_compat` is on, `config.ts` reads `process.env`, and call sites do `c.env?.X ?? getConfig().x` (`middleware/auth.ts:23`), so object bindings are `env`-only while text vars and secrets are reachable both ways. Both are corrected here, which brings the file in line with the two `CLAUDE.md` files it had drifted from.
- **No behaviour change.** Documentation and one example file only; no source, no tests, no deploy.

### Docs — every accepted spec asserts the accessibility criterion, and a green check hides the page that fails it (2026-08-30)

`docs/design/ACCESSIBILITY.md`'s enforcement note recorded what fails the build and what does not, and said nothing about the specifications that assert the requirement in the first place. Measured against the seven accepted feature specification documents themselves rather than a summary of them: **all seven carry the criterion, and not one of them cites a mechanism** (WIC-1584 AC-3; the specification-side counterpart is WIC-15 §8-A).

- **"Only 1 of 7 specs carries an accessibility criterion" is superseded, and requoting it inverts the finding.** `AC-Q3` is in UC-1, UC-2, UC-3, UC-4, the resume spec and onboarding, and the same criterion is named `AC-N7` in UC-5 — seven documents, one wording, all of it SC 1.3.1, and six of the seven record their own status as NOT MET. The figure was true before the WIC-1480 decomposition landed. The gap it describes is not that six specs lack the criterion; it is that seven carry it with nothing behind it. Two of the seven still assert that nothing in the repository can fail them, which the three checks named in the note have made false — routed to the Business Analyst as WIC-1833, those documents not being editable from here.
- **A rendered-outline assertion certifies the composition it renders, not the route it is named after.** `ApplicationsList` skips `h1` → `h3` in every branch at `3a649e1`: `<h1>` at `:136`, then `SavedFilterShortcuts` mounted unconditionally at `:165` rendering `<h3>` at `SavedFilterShortcuts.tsx:113`, with `KanbanBoard`'s `<h2>` column headings arriving only at `:195`. The single CI check that can fail a heading skip is wired to `KanbanBoard` — the component on that very page — and it is green, because its fixture is a hand-written `<h1>Applications</h1>` followed by `<KanbanBoard>`, commented "the `ApplicationsList` shape", which never mounts the sibling that causes the skip. Filed as WIC-1834.
- **Its sibling check is the control that makes this a fixture defect rather than a method defect.** `CoverLetterPreview.test.tsx` builds its fixture the same way, and there the real page does agree — `CoverLetterDetail` goes `<h1>` `:104` → `<h2>`, no skip. The pattern is sound; what is missing is anything that checks a fixture still resembles the page it claims to model, so this one drifted and spent the check's credibility on the way.
- **The note's live-skip count goes from three to four, and the fourth is listed apart rather than appended.** The three already recorded (`ProjectsList`, `ResumeManager`, `ProjectDetail`) skip only in the populated branch, because `EmptyState` gained a `headingLevel` prop under WIC-1417. `ApplicationsList` has no clean branch at all, so it is not another instance of the same shape and grouping it with them would lose the distinction the per-render-branch argument rests on.

No source, test or workflow file is touched here; every code line cited is a measurement of `main` at `3a649e1`.

`docs/design/JOBFIT_CAPS_DECISION_WIC1122.md` §3 is the standing gate on adding a fit-quality colour ramp to the Job Fit Analysis screen — the one forward-looking section of an otherwise historical decision record, and the section `DESIGN_SYSTEM.md` § Enforcement points implementers at. The third citation is in this changelog's WIC-1288 entry and is left as written — it is a dated record of what shipped then.

The sentence was describing which file a commit touched, not citing a specification to obey, so it is now prose naming the branch the file lives on — the unmarked-reference case the script's own scope note calls deliberate. ### Docs — the a11y enforcement decision is ruled, so three implementation cards stop waiting on it (2026-08-30)

`WIC-1192` asked which accessibility checkers `packages/web` should adopt, at what severity, and in what order. It sat unassigned for 11 days while **WIC-1483**, **WIC-1589** and **WIC-1675** queued behind the answer and `ACCESSIBILITY.md` carried an "enforcement status: none" banner. The decision, not the work, was the bottleneck. `A11Y_ENFORCEMENT_RULING.md` rules both halves and hands the config to the implementer.

- **One premise of the card had expired.** WIC-1192 sequenced the `axe-core` option behind the vitest + RTL harness landing. That harness is present at `743cfeb` — `vitest@^4.1.11` plus three `@testing-library/*` packages and 15 test files — so both options are unblocked today and the question is moot.
- **`recommended` and `strict` are identical on this codebase**, measured rather than assumed: `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y@6.10.2` returns the same 50 findings, same 9 rules, same 23 files under either set. `strict` is therefore adopted at zero present cost.
- **Severity is `error` behind a frozen file baseline, not a global `warn`.** Global `warn` never ratchets — a 48th finding is invisible among 47 existing ones — and global `error` red-builds 22 files on the landing commit. The baseline relaxes only today's 23 files, may only shrink, and puts new code at `error` from the first commit.
- **The backlog is real defects, not lint noise, and that is what settles severity.** All 19 `label-has-associated-control` hits were read in source: 14 native `<label>`/control pairs with no `id`+`htmlFor`, 3 group captions wanting `<fieldset>`/`<legend>`, and 2 mislabelled custom components — `WizardContainer.tsx:306`, whose visible label disagrees with `TechStackPicker`'s hard-coded `aria-label` (WCAG 2.5.3), and `ProjectFileEditor.tsx:154`, a `<label>` over a read-only pane with no control at all. **Zero false positives**; the rule also correctly declined to flag the valid nesting at `OutreachComposer.tsx:140`. 47 findings across 22 app-source files independently reproduces WIC-1589's separately-taken count.
- **`axe-core` is hosted in vitest + RTL, not Playwright E2E.** Both hosts are already wired into `deploy.yml`, so neither needs new CI plumbing and the choice turns on the authoring loop: `e2e-tests` is gated behind `lint-and-test`, and Playwright browsers do not launch in the agent development environment, so assertions hosted there cannot be run locally at all. It also covers a blind spot `routeHeadingOutline.test.ts` documents about itself — that source sweep sees only static heading text, and ~30% of `<h1>`/`<h2>` are expression-built.
- **Nothing is enforced yet, and the docs say so.** `ACCESSIBILITY.md`'s enforcement-status note is extended with a pointer to the ruling and an explicit "this is a decision, not a landing"; the note itself stays until the config is in `packages/web/eslint.config.js`. **WIC-1584** still owns replacing it.
- **No behaviour change.** Documentation only; no source, no tests, no deploy.

### Docs — the a11y enforcement ruling is ratified into the architecture record as ADR-011, with two amendments (2026-08-30)

`A11Y_ENFORCEMENT_RULING.md` (one entry above) decided WIC-1192 but was never ratified into `docs/architecture/adr/`, and WIC-1781 asked the Architect to decide and record. ADR-011 adopts both checkers as ruled — jsx-a11y at `strict`/`error` behind a shrink-only baseline, axe-core hosted in vitest + RTL — and does not overturn either half. Re-measuring to ratify surfaced two things the ruling does not account for (WIC-1781, WIC-1192).

- **The ruling's load-bearing measurements reproduce at `ee6c217`, five commits after the `743cfeb` they were taken at.** Same 50 findings / 23 files / 9 rules under both `recommended` and `strict`, identical on **file + rule + line** rather than merely on counts; the §6 baseline table matches row for row; and jsx-a11y `strict` still returns 0 on the WIC-1185 markup with an `<img>`-without-`alt` positive control flagged in the same run. The ruling's own §7 asks that these be re-run rather than copied forward on trust — this is that re-run.
- **`axe-core` reports the WIC-1185 shape as `incomplete`, not as a violation** — so `toHaveNoViolations()`, which reads only `results.violations`, **would pass on the exact defect that motivates adopting axe**. The split is deliberate: with text content present axe says the `aria-label` is "not well supported" and declines to decide; with no text content it is a hard violation. So the shared assertion helper must fail on `incomplete`, with a commented allowlist for rules that are inherently incomplete under jsdom (`color-contrast` has no layout engine to measure). This also makes the ruling's "confirm axe flags the same two components *before* deleting `prohibitedName.ts`" a hard gate rather than prudence — that helper's own header already documented the caveat.
- **The ruling hands off implementation as though unstarted, but PR #226 (WIC-1483) has been open since before it landed** and implements a different baseline shape: 8 rules globally at `warn` pinned by an exact both-directions map test, versus the ruling's 23 files relaxed via an overrides block. The ruling rejected global `warn` because "a 48th finding is invisible among 47" — an objection that does not apply to PR #226 as built, since the 48th fails `jsxA11yBaseline.test.ts` with a precise diff. The ratchet is also strictly stronger: per-file overrides relax the *whole* file, so a new violation in one of the 22 already-baselined app-source files would land at `warn` and pass. PR #226's mechanism is adopted.
- **`strict` is not a superset of `recommended`.** 34 entries (`error` 31, `off` 3) versus 33 (`error` 31, `off` 2), differing on 7 rules: six are option tightenings — `no-static-element-interactions` and `no-noninteractive-tabindex` lose `allowExpressionValues: true` — and the seventh is a loss, `anchor-ambiguous-text` being absent from `strict` entirely. So PR #226 should move to `strict` but **keep** its promotion of that rule. The swap is free at today's counts, leaving `A11Y_BASELINE`, the `--max-warnings 47` ceiling and the three fixture disables untouched.
- **A reopen trigger is recorded, which the ruling omits**: the two tools ceasing to cover disjoint classes, `strict` ceasing to be free, the baseline ceasing to shrink, or Playwright becoming locally runnable. Re-measuring the counts is expected drift and is explicitly *not* grounds to reopen.
- **No behaviour change.** Documentation only; no source, no tests, no deploy. Nothing is enforced until PR #226 lands.

### Fixed — `listObjectKeys` returned nothing on the S3 path, silently disabling three project behaviours (2026-08-30)

`packages/api/src/services/storage.service.ts` implemented `listObjectKeys` only for the Cloudflare Workers R2 binding. Every other function in that module already had an S3 fallback via `@aws-sdk/client-s3`, but this one ended in a bare `return []`. On any S3-configured deployment without the Workers binding — which is how the Node path runs — it therefore reported an empty bucket while `isStorageAvailable()` reported true, so callers could not tell "no files" from "never looked".

- **An existing project file could be overwritten without a conflict.** `createProjectFile` uses the key list as an existence check and throws `ConflictError` when it is non-empty. It was never non-empty, so the check never fired.
- **`deleteProject` orphaned every object it was meant to remove.** It listed the project prefix and passed the result to `deleteObjects`; an empty list deleted nothing while the database row went away regardless.
- **Every project reported a file count of 0** through `listProjects`, `getProject` and `getProjectBySlug`, and `listProjectFiles` returned an empty list.
- **The Workers branch also under-reported.** It took a single `list({ limit: 1000 })` with no cursor loop, so a project holding more than 1000 objects was truncated on that path too — under-counting and under-deleting rather than returning nothing.

`listObjectKeys` now has an `isR2Configured()` branch built on `ListObjectsV2Command` with continuation-token pagination, and the Workers branch loops on its cursor. A truncated page that comes back without a cursor or token terminates the loop rather than spinning. A failed list now propagates instead of being caught, because an empty result is indistinguishable from success to every caller — the defect being fixed here is exactly that confusion.

`deleteObjects` batches at 1000 keys on both paths. That is a consequence of the pagination fix, not an independent change: R2's batch delete rejects more than 1000 keys per call, so a prefix that previously truncated at 1000 would now have handed it more than it accepts.

Covered by `packages/api/test/storage.list-keys.test.ts`, which stubs the S3 client's `send` to reach the branch a Workers-binding fake cannot. Reverting `listObjectKeys` to its previous body fails 8 of its 13 cases; the 5 that survive are the negative controls (unconfigured storage returns `[]`, the loop terminates without a cursor) and the `deleteObjects` batching cases.


### Fixed — the changelog anchor rule had become the collision it was written to prevent (2026-08-29)

`CLAUDE.md`'s "Changelog conventions" told every contributor to place new `[Unreleased]` entries below the current top `### ` entry. That advice works only while few people follow it: "below the top entry" is itself a fixed position, so as adoption grew it became a second shared anchor. The section's own reasoning — that a lower anchor resolves to a different line per branch point — assumes PRs are cut from different commits, which is often not the case here.

- **Measured, not asserted.** Across the 32 open `main`-based PRs touching `CHANGELOG.md`: the top-of-`[Unreleased]` anchor carried **11** hunks and the two lines at the foot of the top entry carried **8** more (#92/#93/#177/#232 and #171/#179/#208/#213) — 19 of 32 PRs at two positions, while everything from the third entry down was uncontended or held a single PR.
- **The rule now says measure, and ships the command that measures.** A copy-pasteable block prints the old-side hunk-start line of every open `main`-based PR so you can insert where nobody else does. It is restricted to `main`-based PRs on purpose: a stacked PR merge-based against `main` reports its parent's hunks too, which inflates every position it touches. This entry is anchored on that measurement.
- **Any figure in the section is perishable and is now labelled as such.** A previous revision recorded "every open PR inserts inside lines 8–58", which was false within hours.
- **The union checks gained the control they were missing.** The post-merge detector was documented as a check on the merge result alone, so a hit could not be attributed. It now says to run the checks on all three inputs and report only what the union _adds_. Over the same 51 PRs simulated against their true bases, the raw output flagged **36** while only **20** were introduced by the merge — the other **16** were already committed on the branch or inherited from its base. The distinction picks the fix: a union-introduced hit means resolve the merge, a pre-existing one means edit the entry, and re-merging will not touch it.
- **Prose change only — no code, no tests, no runtime surface touched.** Both embedded shell blocks were extracted from the merged text and run verbatim against the live repository; the anchor command reproduces the 11 / 4 / 4 figures quoted above. Deliberately not opened with the boilerplate sentence the section names as a known false positive, since a third copy would degrade the check this entry is about.

### Fixed — catalog ambiguities raised on a resume upload were recorded and shown to nobody (2026-08-30)

Closes WIC-1428. UC-2 §7 requires a catalog diff to carry a `pending_review` array for ambiguities needing user input, and the spec's worked example — `PM` → Product Manager / Project Manager — was implemented and did reach the array. Nothing ever displayed it. Resume-triggered changes auto-apply and the row is stamped `status: 'approved'`, while `listDiffs` defaults to `status = 'pending'`, so the diff was never listed; the shipped web client's only accessor takes no parameters, and a diff id is reachable only through that list. The items were persisted correctly and `?status=approved` could return them — this was a client-reachability defect, not data loss.

- **The root cause was one column meaning two things.** `status` was answering both *were the changes applied?* and *is an ambiguity outstanding?*. On the auto-apply path those genuinely diverge — the changes **are** applied **and** an ambiguity **is** open — and `approved` can only express the first. `catalog_diffs.open_review_count` (migration `0020`) now carries the second, and the default list returns `status = 'pending' OR open_review_count > 0`. The existing UI already renders `pendingReviewCount`, so the diff surfaces with its ⚠️ badge and **no client change was needed**.
- **The card's preferred option was measured and rejected.** Leaving such a diff at `status = 'pending'` would have been smaller, but `applyDiff` gates re-application on exactly `status = 'pending'`: an already-applied diff would have been exposed to a second `approve_all`, and `company_catalog` updates increment `application_count` via `sql\`application_count + 1\``, which is not idempotent — plus a `reject_all` that marks the row rejected without un-applying anything. Keeping `status` truthful about the apply decision leaves that guard doing its job. Recorded in the migration header so the next reader does not re-derive it.
- **Resolving or dismissing an item retires the diff.** `resolveDiffItem` recomputes the open count from the decisions actually recorded rather than decrementing, so a client re-submitting a decision for an index it already sent cannot drive the count below the number genuinely left; `approve` and `reject` both count as decided, because dismissing an ambiguity is as resolved as picking an option.
- **History does not flood the list.** The backfill carries outstanding items forward only for rows still `pending` — which the status arm already lists — and leaves every terminal row at `0`, so the change adds no entries to anyone's existing queue. It reports what it touched through `GET DIAGNOSTICS` + `RAISE NOTICE`, readable in the preview deploy log.
- **The fix is shown to be the variable, not just asserted.** A new route test drives the real `processCatalogChange` and the real `listDiffs` behind the real Hono route, and the row the route lists is the row extraction actually inserted for text containing `PM` — not a fixture. Four independent reverts (the list predicate, the extraction write, the resolve write, and a widened arm) each turn it red at an unchanged total of 5 tests, so none of them merely failed to compile. `packages/api` goes 735 → 740 tests with no pre-existing test changed.
- **`@electric-sql/pglite` was deliberately not used.** It resolves locally as an optional peer of drizzle-orm but is declared in no `package.json` on `main`; importing it is how WIC-1433 broke CI at import while the local suite was green. The test fakes only the database, and the fake evaluates drizzle's own rendered SQL so that deleting a predicate arm changes what the rows match.

- **A false status line was corrected.** The modal spec titled its hook section "`useDialogFocusRestore` (shipped, PR #97)". The hook does not exist anywhere under `packages/web/src/`, and PR #97 — with #95 and #115 — is still open. Nothing in that spec has shipped; all six dialogs still lack `Escape`, focus trap and focus restore. **Never write a bare PR state into a design document**; cite a commit, because a PR number is a claim about the future.
- **Three of the 404 spec's four original defects are now stale and are struck**, because `EmptyState` was rewritten by WIC-1155 and WIC-1417. The one the repo actually cites survives and is _stronger_ than when written: what was a hardcoded `<h3>` is now the closed union `EmptyStateHeadingLevel = 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6`, so `1` is excluded by the type system rather than by convention.
- **A new contrast defect was found while re-measuring**, and flagged rather than absorbed: `JobFitAnalysis.tsx:238` still renders the Partial Matches card with a raw `border-l-4 border-yellow-500`. WIC-1146 tokenised the Gaps card immediately below it and measured that exact Tailwind value at **1.92:1**, against the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 bar its own `gapSeverity.ts` documents for the `mark` role. Not a `GapSeverity` render site, so the reconciliation missed it.
- **`docs/design/doc-reference-audit.py` is wired into `deploy.yml`** and fails the build on any `SOMETHING.md` cited in `docs/` that resolves nowhere in the repo. Fenced code blocks are stripped first, so an example filename in a snippet is not credited as a citation — the same defect the route-title audit hit with comments. Six controls: the clean tree passes, deleting each of the three ported docs reproduces its original dangling reference by citing file and line, a fenced fake passes, and a prose fake fails.
- **The checker found a fourth dangling reference on its first run**, outside the design docs it was written for: `docs/analytics/fleet-health-2026-08-26-1152Z.md` cited a fleet-oauth-outage write-up that exists nowhere. The unresolvable pointer was removed and the methodological claim it supported left intact. The audit was **not** narrowed to `docs/design/` to keep this PR green — scoping a checker around its first true positive is how checkers become decorative.
- **The durable Overline ruling is now a rule in `DESIGN_SYSTEM.md`, not just a ported file.** WIC-1629 asked for one specific thing — the ruling that _Overline is the wrong instrument for a primary result_ — to land as a subsection under § Typography → Type Scale, and said explicitly that the rest of `JOBFIT_CAPS_DECISION_WIC1122.md` is a shipped implementation spec that does **not** need porting. Porting the file alone would have satisfied the citation checker while leaving the actual ruling undiscoverable: the type-scale table records _what Overline is_ and nothing recorded _when it is wrong to reach for_. The subsection is now there, cross-linked both ways with `CONTENT_STYLE.md` § _ALL CAPS is a typographic treatment, not casing_, which governs how caps are applied and is a different question from where caps belong. Re-measured at `a59b869`: Overline is the smallest step in the scale (10px/600), and the confidence caption under the overall-fit recommendation is `text-sm` — 14px, `JobFitAnalysis.tsx:162` — so an Overline verdict would render the answer smaller than its own footnote.
- **Two false claims were removed from the audit script's own docstring.** It advertised that it "checks that a cited _section_ anchor is plausible". It does not — `main()` compares filenames and nothing else; there is no anchor logic in the file. It also left its matching scope unstated, which reads as broader coverage than exists: only _marked-up_ references are checked, so a bare unbackticked `FOO.md` in prose escapes the audit entirely. That limitation is deliberate — matching bare filenames misfires on ordinary sentences — but an unstated limit in a checker's own description is how a green check gets over-read. Both corrected, and the scope is now stated first.
- **The first draft of the audit hung a CI step.** It called `rglob` per reference, which walks `node_modules` for every _missing_ file, and a missing file never short-circuits. Indexing markdown basenames in one walk took it from a >2-minute timeout to 0.085s. Noted because it was caught by a control, not by review.

### Fixed — a catalog merge target listed as its own source destroyed itself (2026-08-26)

Found while reviewing the `ANY` repair below and filed separately, because that repair is what makes this reachable: every merge previously died at the source read before any write ran, so the merge **write** path had never executed. Nothing — Zod schema or service — required the target id to be absent from the source list, and `sourcesWhere` is built from `sourceIds` alone and is exactly the predicate the merge deletes by (WIC-1395).

- **A target that was also a source was deleted by its own merge.** Measured against a real Postgres, not a mock: `mergeCompanies(['X'], 'X')` returned **200 OK** with company `X` already `isDeleted` and its `applicationCount` doubled — a silent destructive success, the caller is told it worked. `mergeJobFitTags(['T'], 'T')` was worse: the tag delete is a **hard** delete, so the row was gone unrecoverably, after which the `updated!` re-read was `undefined` and `toJobFitTagDTO` threw a `TypeError` — surfacing as an opaque **500** rather than anything diagnosable. `mergeTechStackTags` is structurally identical.
- **Not a security issue and nothing was losing data.** The WIC-1365 tenancy scoping holds — a caller can only destroy their own records, verified by execution — and `packages/web` has no call site for any of these endpoints, so there is no client to trigger it. This was a latent trap, not an incident: it mattered because the fix below ships these endpoints working for the first time, and a very plausible first client (a multi-select where the survivor is also ticked) would hit it.
- **The existing `assertMergeSources` guard was extended rather than a second one added**, so all three services keep a single validation call and reject with a `400` before any predicate is built or any row is read. This also retires the `updated!` non-null assertion as a hazard: the target can no longer be deleted by its own merge, which was the only path that made that re-read empty.
- **15 new tests assert the surviving row, not just the rejection.** A rejection-only test would pass against a version that rejects _after_ deleting, which is precisely the failure being pinned. Each of the three functions gets the sole-source case, the realistic multi-select case (target ticked alongside a genuine source), and single-user mode — all asserting the stored row is byte-identical to what went in — plus a non-overlapping merge that must still succeed, which is what separates a correct guard from an over-broad one, and a non-overlapping merge with a foreign-owned row sitting in the store, which must be neither counted nor written. The write path needed a new double: `stubDb` cannot model deletion and `stubOwnedRow` has no transaction, so `stubRowStore` backs a mutable row store that honours where-clauses through `update` and `delete`. Reverting the guard fails exactly 9 of the 15 — the six non-overlapping merges are the regression guards, meant to pass either way — but the reversal is _not_ what proves the row assertions do any work, because `rejects` fails first and the row check is never reached. Moving the throw to _after_ the transaction is what proves it: the call still rejects with a byte-identical error, and 9 fail on the row state itself. The two remaining terms of the double's own contract are pinned by the foreign-owner case, which is the only test that fails if `update` ignores its where-clause, or if row visibility drops the tenancy term and matches on bare id membership.

### Fixed — all three catalog merge endpoints returned 500 for every request (2026-08-26)

The three merge services read their source rows with a raw template, `` sql`${companyCatalog.id} = ANY(${sourceIds})` ``. Drizzle expands a JS array interpolated into a `sql` template as a comma-separated **parameter list**, not as a single array parameter, so that rendered `"company_catalog"."id" = ANY(($1, $2))`. `($1, $2)` is a row constructor and `= ANY(...)` requires an array or a subquery, so Postgres rejected the statement outright — `POST /api/catalog/companies/merge`, `.../tags/job-fit/merge` and `.../tags/tech-stack/merge` all threw at the source read, for every input, in both single-user and scoped mode (WIC-1377).

- **The predicate is now `inArray`**, which renders `"company_catalog"."id" in ($1, $2)` — the spelling every other multi-id query in the codebase already uses. `= ANY(` occurred **only** in these three functions and nowhere else in `src/`, which is what made it findable.
- **The tenancy scoping from the merge fix below is untouched.** Only the id term changed; the `and(...)` wrapper and the `userId ?` conditional are byte-for-byte as WIC-1365 left them. The ordering mattered: before that fix, this broken read was accidentally _masking_ the cross-tenant write, because the unscoped target read succeeded and then the source read threw before any `UPDATE`/`DELETE` ran. Repairing `ANY` first would have made the WIC-1365 vulnerability live.
- **An empty source list is now rejected with a 400 instead of a 500.** On the pinned drizzle-orm (`^0.30.10`) `inArray(col, [])` does not render `false` as newer versions do — it throws `inArray requires at least one value` while the query is being built. The routes already enforce `.min(1)` (`catalog.routes.ts:70,75`), so this only reaches a direct service call, but it now fails the way the route would.
- **Nothing in the suite could have caught the original defect, so the new tests assert the rendered SQL.** `catalog.service.test.ts` mocks `getDb()` wholesale and `catalog.routes.test.ts` mocks the service, so no statement ever reaches an engine; worse, the WIC-1365 tenancy assertions inspect the `user_id` term and the bound params, which are _identical_ for the broken and the fixed spelling. Only the emitted string distinguishes them. 15 new tests (five cases across all three merge functions) pin the `in (...)` rendering for the multi-id, single-id and single-user cases, assert `ANY(` appears in no mode, and cover the empty-list guard; reverting the service fix fails exactly those 15.


### Added — a job fit analysis is now written down, so the workflow checklist's fourth step can tick (2026-08-30)

`POST /api/catalog/job-fit/analyze` computed a result, returned it, and stored nothing. There was no `job_fit_analyses` table, and `AnalyzeJobFitResponse` carried no id — so the caller could not name the analysis it had just spent an LLM call and a rate-limit slot on, `WorkflowChecklist`'s `hasFitAnalysis` and `fitScore` props were unreachable by construction rather than merely unwired, and the `job_fit_analysis_id` columns on four tables referenced nothing. ADR-012 ruled that analyses are persisted, not that the columns are removed (WIC-1652).

- **The table existed on paper for months.** `DATA_MODEL.md` has given `interview_preps` a `job_fit_analysis_id TEXT REFERENCES job_fit_analyses(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` since UC-7 was written, and lists the relationship in its index — but it never *defined* `job_fit_analyses`, which is how a documented foreign key regressed to bare `TEXT` and passed review. The definition is now in `DATA_MODEL.md` alongside the DDL, with the omission recorded rather than quietly filled in.
- **`fitScore` is not a new score.** It is the weighted required-skill match percentage the UC-3 cascade already computed inside `computeRecommendation` and discarded — exact matches count 1, alias/related count 0.5. `computeMatchFraction` is now extracted and shared, so the tier and the percentage rendered beside it are read off one number and cannot contradict each other the way WIC-1309's blurbs and counts did.
- **`null` fitScore means unscored, not zero.** It is `null` exactly when `recommendation` is `null` — the catalog was empty, or the job description named no required skills. A `NOT NULL` column would have forced a `0` that renders as "0% match", conflating a result with its absence.
- **`applicationId` is optional and nullable, deliberately.** Analysing a bare job description with no application in hand is a shipped flow, so `NOT NULL` would have rejected requests that are valid today. When supplied it is resolved against the caller's own applications *before* the rate-limit slot is taken and before the model is called, so an unresolvable id costs nothing; the 404 does not distinguish "no such application" from "not yours", because the lookup is owner-scoped and telling them apart would make the endpoint an existence oracle.
- **Migration 0022 nulls the dangling referrers before adding the constraints, and the order is asserted.** Every existing `job_fit_analysis_id` value names an analysis that has never existed, so `ADD CONSTRAINT` would fail on real data — a migration that passes on an empty preview database and breaks in production. A test pins that each `UPDATE ... SET job_fit_analysis_id = NULL` precedes the `ADD CONSTRAINT`, that all four FKs are `ON DELETE SET NULL` (read off the drizzle table objects, not grepped from the source), and that 0022 is registered in `_journal.json` — a migration the runner never reads is not a migration.
- **A migration whose journal `when` is not the newest is skipped in total silence, and this one was.** `drizzle-orm/pg-core/dialect.js:56` applies a file only when `Number(lastDbMigration.created_at) < migration.folderMillis`, comparing against the **single newest** applied row rather than checking each file's own hash — and `created_at` is the journal's `when`. The first cut here was numbered `0020` with `when: 1777620258000`, which is byte-identical to the `when` on an open PR's `0020_backfill_catalog_diffs_user_id` and below another open PR's `0021`. Both had already run against the shared preview database, so this migration never executed there — and `db:migrate` printed *"Migrations complete."*, exited 0, and the whole deploy went green. It was caught only because `verify-rls.mjs` derives its table list from the live schema and `job_fit_analyses` was absent from the 21 tables it printed. Renumbered to `0022` with a strictly greater `when`, and the journal now carries an asserted invariant — unique `idx`, strictly increasing `when`, and this migration last — which fails on the post-merge state that the original numbering would have produced.
- **`GET /api/catalog/job-fit/analyses` is the read half.** Without it an analysis is stored but unfindable, so `ApplicationDetail` still could not tell whether an application had been analysed. It returns summaries rather than whole analyses, owner-scoped, with the `applicationId` filter applied *in addition to* the owner term and never instead of it.
- **8 service mutants and 7 route/schema negative controls, each killed with the collection count gated.** Deleting the insert, returning an id that was never stored, widening the ownership `and` to `or`, accepting an unresolvable id, dropping the owner term from the list read, re-weighting `fitScore` away from the cascade, skipping persistence on the catalog-empty exit, and conflating unscored with zero all go red; so do removing the new route, dropping `applicationId` from the request schema, and not passing the caller id through. Every mutant collected the full baseline, so none was a non-compiling green (WIC-1610). API suite 33 files / 768 tests, up from 31 / 735.
- **AC-2 and AC-3 — the checklist tick and the two `recommended` badges — are the web half and are not in this change.** They stack on PR #217, which wires `WorkflowChecklist`'s other props and is still open. Tracked separately; the API and schema this needed are what landed here.

### Added — the per-route `document.title` convention is in the repo, re-measured, and cross-linked (2026-08-27)

`ROUTE_TITLE_CONVENTION.md` was cited as a constraint by WIC-1571's ticket but existed only in the UI/UX Developer's workspace directory, which is not the repository. The implementer looked, correctly reported that the file did not exist, and had to invent a justification for the copy instead. The design work had been done and then had no effect (WIC-1582).

- **The document now lives at `docs/design/ROUTE_TITLE_CONVENTION.md`**, and its route table was re-measured against `f457cc3` rather than ported as written. That caught four drifts: `/cover-letters/new`'s heading moved from `CoverLetterGenerator.tsx:181` to a page `<h1>` at `CoverLetterNew.tsx:47` (WIC-1571); the 404's heading is `That page couldn't be found`, not the `Page not found` the table specified; `/resumes/:resumeId/exports` was added after the table was written and had no row; and `/job-fit-analysis`'s two stage headings moved line. Corrections are struck inline, not silently rewritten, so the drift stays auditable.
- **Its central premise had inverted.** The document was written against a tree where `NotFound.tsx` set `document.title` and everything else did not. At `f457cc3` **no file under `packages/web/src/` writes `document.title` at all** — the 404's effect was removed and the shared mechanism that was to replace it was never built. So acceptance criterion 5, which told the implementer to delete that effect and move two assertions in `e2e/not-found.spec.ts`, pointed at code and assertions that no longer exist. AC5 is restated; the spec has no title assertion today and gains one.
- **Two new rules.** A modal never changes `document.title`, and the title mirrors the `<h1>` that `ROUTE_HEADING_OUTLINE.md` assigns to the _route_ — needed because `/applications/:id/prep` renders a second `<h1>` from inside the `QuickReferenceExport` overlay (`QuickReferenceExport.tsx:89`), filed as a heading-outline follow-up.
- **The dependency is now cross-linked in both directions.** `ROUTE_HEADING_OUTLINE.md` §6 said the file did not exist; it now points at it and states the live obligation — changing a route's `<h1>` requires updating the title table in the same PR, because every string in that table is copied from it.
