- **The enforcement is where a build actually checks it** — the invariants live in `src/` as an exported `UnitBrandInvariants` tuple, not as `@ts-expect-error` lines in a test. `packages/api/tsconfig.json` excludes `test/` and Vitest transpiles without type-checking, so assertions written in the test file would have been verified by **nothing**. Confirmed by mutation: collapsing the two `__unit` literals produces `TS2344` in both packages. The mirrored copies are pinned byte-identical by a test, likewise mutation-checked.
- **Six documentation declarations corrected** — five `COMPONENT_SPECS.md` `relevanceScore` sites were simply wrong against shipped code, not describing a second convention, and are now `0-1`; only `STARStoryBank`'s is a genuine 0-100 site. `matchConfidence` (0-100) and `confidence` (0-1) were one quantity under two names in two units, reconciled to `confidence`. `API_CONTRACTS.md:557` no longer calls a ratio a "percentage" — the corpus was swept and that was the only such site.
- **`PrepStory.relevanceScore` is renamed, not converted** — it is persisted as `integer` and produced by a prompt asking for a 0-100 integer, so converting it means a data migration with failure modes strictly worse than the naming problem. `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` moves no data. The contract documents the target name; **the wire field is still `relevanceScore` on `main`** until the backend and frontend children land, and the deviations table says so in one authoritative place.
- **No behaviour change ships here.** WIC-1514's files (`DashboardStats.tsx`, `types/application.ts`) are deliberately untouched — that card owns them. `completeness` (0-100) is recorded as a known, deliberate conformance gap rather than silently ignored.
- **This entry was moved off the top anchor** to comply with the WIC-1543 convention added below. It originally sat at the first `### ` heading under the backfill note, and was knocked into `CONFLICTING` twice in one day from that line — by #169, then by #178. Re-anchoring narrowed the window but did not close it: this PR was knocked out twice more *from the re-anchored line*, by #185, #186 and #187, because a PR cut from the same `main` resolves "below the top entry" to the same line. That residual is documented in `CLAUDE.md`; what is new here is that a PR sitting in `REVIEW_REQUIRED` can re-collide faster than its author can push a fix. **Nine collisions in ~28h, and the last four arrived in one 85-minute window** — #195, #196, #197 and #198 all landed between this PR being declared `MERGEABLE`/7-of-7-green and the next check on it. Re-anchoring reduces the *rate* and nothing else: any PR cut from the same `main` resolves "below the top entry" to the same line, so the collision probability scales with merge traffic, not with where the author aims. That is the measurement ADR-009 (#190) rests on, and the reason a per-PR fix cannot be the remedy.

### Docs — All ten `cursor` parameter rows in API_CONTRACTS.md now say the cursor is opaque (2026-08-27)

`docs/architecture/API_CONTRACTS.md` had six `| cursor |` query-parameter rows, each carrying `(opaque — see [Pagination](#pagination))` inline. PR #112 documented four more paginated report endpoints and took the count to ten, and three of the four new rows read a bare `Pagination cursor`.

- **A consistency gap, not a contract error — and it is worth being exact about that.** The three endpoints (`needs-action`, `stale`, `closed-loop`) sit under the UC-5 section preamble, which already states opacity for all three and tells clients to pass the cursor back verbatim. No endpoint was mis-specified and no client reading the section could be misled. The cost fell on the reader who deep-links to a single endpoint heading and sees a bare row with no qualifier and no link back to § Pagination — which is how these tables are actually read.
- **Why uniformity is worth a PR here.** `parseCursor`'s docstring justifies its `400` on cursors being opaque _everywhere_, and after the entry below that argument rests on § Pagination rather than on per-row text. Keeping the rows uniform keeps the cheapest confirmation of that claim cheap.
- **The shared reports table at the top of § UC-5 is deliberately left alone.** It reads "Opaque page token, issued by the server as `nextCursor`" — already correct, and better suited to a table that covers three endpoints at once than the per-endpoint phrasing would be.
- Documentation only. No source, schema, wire, or test change.


### Docs — Reformatting a changelog line you did not change is enough to republish a retracted claim (2026-08-30)

The changelog rules in `CLAUDE.md` treated "both sides revised the same entry" as a collision between two *substantive* edits. It is not. `merge=union` grades edits by position, so a branch that only restyles a line — `*emphasis*` to `_emphasis_`, the shape `prettier --parser markdown` produces — collides exactly as hard as one that rewrites it.

- **The damaging pairing is the likely one.** Edits to an already-shipped entry are overwhelmingly corrections, because that is the only reason anyone reopens one. So the collision is normally a branch's stale copy against `main`'s corrected copy — and union emits the branch's first, printing the retracted claim above its own retraction.
- **Measured on a real instance, since caught and repaired.** At `main` `3b0c0d3`, PR #209 at head `fdd800d` rewrote nine pre-existing lines with emphasis-only changes. `main` had corrected one of them four hours earlier in `70396b0`, so the merge carried that bullet twice, uncorrected copy first — confirmed byte-identical to a real `git merge origin/main` in a scratch worktree. Routed to the branch owner as WIC-1884 and fixed the same day in `cdb1c24`, which reverted all nine; re-measured at head `2085803`, the union introduces nothing. The mode is documented here on the strength of that measurement, not because the branch is still broken.
- **Four open PRs still carry the pattern, 151 lines between them** — #299 (91), #261 (48), #249 (10), #226 (2), measured at `main` `3b0c0d3`. **None collides today.** They are dormant only because `main` has not touched those lines yet; taking a dormant line and synthesising a `main` that corrects it moves the union from one copy to two, with the untouched control staying at one. Re-measure before quoting this roster — the #209 entry moved from nine lines to zero while this entry was being written.
- **A second, independent reason the formatter stays scoped to `packages/**`.** The first was that prettier strips the blank line above every `### ` heading and re-arms the weld on every entry at once (WIC-1732). This one is that it rewrites pre-existing lines, and in a union-merged file every rewritten line is a collision candidate. Widening the glob to root `CHANGELOG.md` remains prohibited.
- **The byte-exact conservation check is blind to this class.** The two copies differ — that is the point — so nothing is lost and no count moves. Only the normalised-prefix bullet check finds it, which is the concrete case that normalisation was worth paying for.
- Convention text only; nothing executable moved, and no changelog line already on `main` was restyled by this entry.

### Docs — A union-driver "clean" merge is not a correct one, so the changelog rules now say how to check

`CLAUDE.md` → "Changelog conventions" told you how to _diagnose_ a `CHANGELOG.md` conflict GitHub sees and local tools do not, and then stopped at "keep both sides". That left the step where the damage actually happens undocumented: `merge=union` resolves the file silently, and its resolution can be wrong in ways no tool reports.

- **Two failure modes, both of which reached `main`.** When both branches revise the _same existing_ entry, union keeps both revisions and ships two contradictory descriptions of one change (WIC-1561, fixed by #181). And when a branch inserts an entry directly above an existing one, union can consume the blank line at the seam, welding a `### ` heading onto the previous entry's last bullet — _even though both parents had that blank line_ (WIC-1567, fixed by #185). Neither shows a conflict marker; neither fails a build.
- **A detector, not a warning.** The section now carries a short `python3` heredoc that reports duplicated bullets and headings missing a preceding blank line, to be run after any merge touching `CHANGELOG.md`. It was checked against a planted weld rather than only run — the pre-existing state of this file gave it two true positives (the two entries below, welded on `main` before this change and repaired here), and a synthetic case confirms it fires on a fresh one.
- **Resolution is per bullet.** Stated explicitly, because take-ours/take-theirs is the tempting shortcut and is always wrong here: each side normally holds an entry the other genuinely lacks, which is why the driver exists at all.
- **Counts in prose are called out as rot-prone.** An entry written this week said "all six `cursor` rows" and was stale within the day when PR #112 documented four more paginated endpoints. Cite the rule the file states, not a tally taken by grep.
- Documentation and changelog formatting only. No source, schema, wire, or test change.
- **The rule caught its own merge.** Bringing `main` in after #185 landed reproduced failure mode 2 exactly: the driver reported a clean resolution and had welded this entry onto the one below. The detector in this change found it; nothing else would have.

### Docs — `parseCursor`'s rationale no longer cites an encoding the API contract stopped publishing (2026-08-26)

`packages/api/src/lib/pagination.ts` justified rejecting a malformed cursor with a `400` by pointing at `API_CONTRACTS.md`: the catalog endpoints' encoding was _published_ rather than called opaque, so a hand-crafted base64url offset was a legitimate input that still worked, and the `400` therefore only ever caught broken clients. PR #120 (`172802b`) removed that published encoding. The citation has been wrong on `main` ever since (WIC-1567).

- **The premise died; the conclusion got stronger.** With the encoding unpublished, a hand-crafted cursor is not a supported input _at all_ — `API_CONTRACTS.md` § Pagination now says "a cursor this API did not issue is not a supported input: it may return an error rather than a page of results". The docstring quotes that sentence instead of the old inference, so the argument is now grounded in text a reader can go and check.
- **Why a comment was worth a PR.** This is the load-bearing rationale for the status code, not a stray aside. A maintainer who follows the citation finds it false, and the maintainer who doubts the citation is exactly the one who then doubts the `400`.
- **The catalog is no longer singled out, because nothing makes it special now.** No `cursor` row publishes the encoding any more; the old wording's "even for the catalog endpoints" survives only as a one-line note on what the paragraph used to argue, so the removed reasoning is not helpfully "restored" by someone who remembers it.
- **The rationale cites § Pagination, not a row count.** An earlier draft of this entry and of the docstring both said "all six `cursor` rows" — a number that was correct when written and stale within the day, because PR #112 documented four more paginated report endpoints and took it to ten. A count of parameter rows tracks how many endpoints are documented, which is not what the argument needs; § Pagination's blanket "treat cursors as opaque" is the durable citation, so both now rest on that instead.
- **Verified as the only carrier.** `git grep` over `packages/`, `docs/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/` finds no other source or doc asserting the cursor encoding is published; the two remaining `base64` mentions in `API_CONTRACTS.md` are the `base64Content` file-upload fields, and `base64url` no longer appears in that file at all. `.claude/CLAUDE.md` still describes the encoding, correctly — it is an internal implementation reference, not the client-facing contract.
- **Comment-only.** No behaviour, no wire values, no test expectations change. `pagination.test.ts`'s leak guard scans `src/services/`, not `src/lib/`, so it is untouched either way.
- Mirror of WIC-1566, which fixes the same drift from the other end: PR #112's changelog claims two encoding-leak edits that #120 in fact landed first.

### Fixed — EmptyState's heading level is a prop, so it stops skipping h2 on every page (2026-08-26)

`EmptyState` rendered its heading as a hardcoded `<h3>`, and all four call sites place it directly beneath the page `<h1>` — so every rendering skipped a level. WIC-1155 (#99) had just made that outline load-bearing by removing the `role="region"` landmark that used to (badly) label this block, leaving the heading as the component's only accessible entry point. Heading-level skips break the outline screen-reader users navigate by (`H` in NVDA/JAWS, the VoiceOver rotor), which for these four pages is the entire structure of an otherwise contentless screen (WIC-1417).

- **A prop, not `s/h3/h2/`.** A tag swap is correct at all four call sites _today_, which is what makes it a trap: a shared presentational component cannot know how deeply its host nests it, and the first time someone renders it inside a card or a tab panel that already owns an `<h2>`, a hardcoded `<h2>` is wrong in the other direction — and the next person hardcodes a third value. That is the failure WIC-1155 just closed, a component-level constant standing in for a decision belonging to the host page.
- **The default is `2` and the prop stays optional**, so all four call sites become correct with no call-site change and the fix is genuinely additive. Requiring it was considered and rejected: a required prop with one obvious answer gets filled in with whatever the neighbouring file passed, which buys ceremony rather than an explicit decision. `1` is not a legal value — the page `<h1>` names the route, and an empty state is never the route.
- **The size does not follow the level.** `text-h4` stays pinned at every level, and there is a test that fails if the two are ever re-coupled. Semantic depth depends on where the host renders the component; visual weight does not.
- **The tests were checked against a mutant, not just run.** Reverting the default to `3` fails exactly two assertions and nothing else, so the new suite discriminates rather than passing vacuously. `NotFound.test.tsx`'s negative control — which rendered `EmptyState` to prove a rejected 404 design really was defective — was pinned to `getByRole('heading', { level: 3 })`; it now asserts level 2, and its sibling assertion sweeps levels 2–6 instead of pinning one, so the control keeps discriminating now that the level is caller-controlled. The defect it names is "the top heading is not an `h1`", which no value of this prop can produce.
- **Sibling components were measured, not assumed.** Of the 30 heading-bearing components in `packages/web/src/components/`, only 4 have more than one render site, and only 2 have a live skip: `CoverLetterPreview` (`h1 → h3` under `CoverLetterDetail`, correct under `CoverLetterGenerator`) and `ApplicationCard` (an `h3` that is a _sibling_ of `KanbanColumn`'s own `h3`). `PersonalInfoForm` is already correct at both of its depths, and `ApplicationForm`'s case is `/applications/new` having no heading at all, which is WIC-1099. The remaining 26 are single-call-site feature panels whose level is effectively part of their page's outline and belongs in that page's audit (WIC-1483), not behind a prop. Filed as follow-up rather than swept in here.
- Specified in `docs/design/COMPONENT_SPECS.md` §10 → Accessibility → "Heading level", extending the block WIC-1155 rewrote. Presentation only; no wire, schema, or behavioural change, and no visual change for sighted users.

### Fixed — a docs-only `[skip ci]` commit could break the docs audits and never run them (2026-08-30)

Three audits wired into the required `Lint & Test` job gate only documentation: `docs/design/doc-reference-audit.py`, `route-title-table-audit.py`, and `wireframe-casing-audit.py`. A docs-only commit is therefore both the only change that can break them and exactly the change `[skip ci]` is meant to wave through — `skip-ci-guard.yml` permits docs-only and workflow-only skips as the deliberate no-deploy route. But `[skip ci]` suppresses the `push` and `pull_request` events, so when the marker is present those audits never run: `f07b9f6` landed a dangling `ADR-007` citation via a direct `[skip ci]` push and `main` went red unseen, and every branch rebased onto it inherited the failing required check through no fault of its own (PR #141, #159, #161, #256). New `.github/workflows/docs-audit.yml` runs the three audits on triggers `[skip ci]` cannot suppress — `pull_request_target` for the PR route, and an hourly `schedule` on `main` for the direct-push route that a PR gate cannot see — which decouples the audits from the skip-ci mechanism at its source rather than inverting the guard's runtime-code predicate. The audits stay pure-stdlib `python3`, so the job is near-free, and the docs `[skip ci]` no-deploy route stays untaxed (WIC-1867).

### Changed — Skip-CI sweeper publishes the required status on the PR event, not just on the cron (2026-08-26)

`skip-ci-sweep` is the only required status context on `main`, and it was published solely by the sweeper's `*/15` cron. Measured 2026-08-26: that cron actually delivered ~1/hr with multi-hour gaps (GitHub throttles frequent schedules under congestion), so every fresh PR head sat `pending` — unmergeable — until the next sweep, and the gate was being hand-cranked (37 `workflow_dispatch` in 22h). Added a `pull_request_target: [opened, synchronize, reopened]` trigger so the status is published on the event that creates the need; the schedule stays as the backstop it was designed to be (WIC-1558).

- **Security property unchanged.** The job still has no `actions/checkout` and no `run:` step, so `pull_request_target` — which grants a base-repo token — executes no PR head code, even from a fork. It only reads the changed-file list and head commit message over the API, exactly as under `schedule`.
- **Why the schedule stays.** Edge triggers do not retro-fire (PRs already open when this merges) and `pull_request_target` loads the workflow from the base tip (a PR whose base predates the file gets no run). The cron covers both — it is now the backstop, not the primary path.
- **Concurrency now coalesces.** Each pass re-evaluates the full open-PR set from live API state, so a newer run subsumes an older one; `cancel-in-progress: true` keeps the per-event trigger from queueing as deep as the open-PR count under a push burst. Fail-closed is preserved — an unreached head stays `pending` until the successor posts it.

### Docs — Changelog entries have an insertion convention, because the union driver never reached GitHub (2026-08-26)

`CHANGELOG.md` has carried `merge=union` since the driver was added, and the `.gitattributes` comment says it "keeps both sides' entries instead of conflicting". That is true of the _local_ three-way merge and of nothing else: GitHub computes mergeability without consulting `.gitattributes`, so PRs kept reporting `CONFLICTING / DIRTY` on a file every local tool called clean. `CLAUDE.md` now has a `## Changelog conventions` section stating the rule, the mechanism behind it, and how to reproduce what GitHub sees (WIC-1543).

- **The rule is one line: new `[Unreleased]` entries go below the current top `### ` entry, not above it.** Entries inside a release are same-day and effectively unordered, so ordering is not lost.
- **Why the top of the section is a _guaranteed_ collision, not a likely one.** Every conflict measured is the same insertion collision at the first `### ` heading under the backfill note, with an **empty merge base** and pure additions on both sides — hence "keep both", hence the recurrence. That anchor is branch-point independent: the backfill note has sat above it since `1ea6186`, so every open PR resolves "top of `[Unreleased]`" to the same line regardless of when it was cut.
- **Why a lower anchor actually helps, and its limit.** "Below the current top entry" resolves to a different line per branch point, so only PRs cut from the identical `main` can still collide. It reduces the collision set; it does not abolish it, and the section says so rather than overselling the rule. Measured on PR #174 — it edited `CHANGELOG.md` alongside three open PRs and added zero new conflicts, where #169, #170 and #172 each took the top anchor and #170 alone broke #165 and #166.
- **The diagnosis recipe is included because the obvious tools lie.** `git merge`, `git merge-tree` and `git pull` all apply the union driver and report clean. Only `git merge-file` on extracted blobs reproduces GitHub's verdict, and only with a positive control — a wrong path or a stale `origin` otherwise produces a convincing false "clean". Re-confirmed against `main` at `94375c1` while writing this: #165 and #166 each show exactly one conflict hunk, control clean.
- **Resolution guidance is carried with it** — keep both sides, merge `main` in, never rebase, because many open PRs here are stacked and rebasing a parent invalidates every child.
- **This entry is itself anchored below the top entry**, not above it. Docs-only; no runtime, schema, or wire change.

### Docs — Every `curl` example in API_CONTRACTS.md now sends a token, against a chosen host (2026-08-26)

Twelve of the sixteen `curl` examples in `docs/architecture/API_CONTRACTS.md` were hardcoded to `http://localhost:3000` and sent **no `Authorization` header** — a combination that only runs under the local auth bypass, which needs **both** `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` absent. Copied against any real environment all twelve return `401`. This closes the residue WIC-1330 deliberately deferred: at the time four in-flight PRs held hunks in the same file and the note said so rather than fixing it.

- **The header is on all twelve, not just the ones that would 401 loudest.** An example that omits `Authorization` documents its endpoint as unauthenticated, and none of these are — `/api/*` is wrapped by the JWT middleware at `app.ts:103`, with only the three `/api/auth/*` routes exempt.
- **The host moved into `$API_BASE`, and the token into `$TOKEN`**, defined once in a new "Running the `curl` examples" block under Authentication. Previously the host was baked into twelve URLs, so "run these against production" meant twelve edits and the document had no single place to state which host it meant. `$API_BASE` carries the `/api` prefix, matching the rows of the Base URL table exactly, so any row can be pasted in unchanged.
- **This replaces a caveat with a fix.** The paragraph added by WIC-1330 told the reader to swap the host _and_ add the header themselves. That was honest while the file was contended, but it documented the defect instead of removing it.
- **The four `https://api.example.com/v1/...` examples under Applications are deliberately untouched** — a separate older surface, and they already carry an `Authorization` header. Noted inline so the inconsistency reads as scoped rather than missed.
- **Verified as shell, not by eye.** All twelve blocks were extracted and parsed with `bash -n`, and the variable expansion checked, so no line-continuation or quoting was broken by the rewrite. Docs-only; no endpoint, schema, or wire value changes.

### Fixed — Match and gap section headings now name the skills they count (2026-08-26)

`✅ Strong Matches (7)` counted **nice-to-have** skills without saying so, while the fit summary a few rows above it counted required skills only. So the screen could show "You match 5 of 6 required skills." above "✅ Strong Matches (7)" — 7 > 6, with nothing on screen to explain it. `⚠️ Partial Matches` and `❌ Gaps` had the identical defect. This is the residue of the WIC-1301 entry below, not a regression from it: before that change the summary opened "Strong match — ", so the two lines shared a noun and read as two statements of one quantity that **disagreed**; removing the prefix left the fault **undisclosed** rather than contradictory (WIC-1528).

- **The heading names its populations** — `✅ Strong Matches (5 required, 2 nice-to-have)`, required always first, **the zero term omitted** rather than rendered as "0 nice-to-have". The noun is elided because the heading supplies it, so the subtotals do not pluralise. Formatted by `packages/web/src/constants/skillCount.ts` (new), read by all three sections so they cannot drift into three formats.
- **Deliberately not a second fraction** — `(7 of 9 skills)` was rejected. It would put a second `X of Y` beside the summary's `5 of 6 required skills` with a different numerator _and_ denominator: the WIC-1288 "one word, two meanings" collision restated in numerals, with no qualifier to tell the two fractions apart. Splitting each section by `isRequired` was rejected too — it doubles the card chrome and still does not reconcile the numbers, because `computeSummary` counts required strong **plus** required partial.
- **The subtotals are not meant to sum to the summary's numerator, and must not be "fixed" into equality** — they are different populations and now say so. Forcing agreement would make the heading report something other than the rows beneath it. Recorded in the spec so the next reader does not re-derive it.
- **The fixture blind spot is closed** — every mock pinning this screen was all-`isRequired`, the one shape where "count of matches" and "count of required matches" coincide, which is why this survived WIC-1288 and WIC-1301 unseen. `MOCK_ANALYSIS_RESPONSE` now carries a nice-to-have strong match and a nice-to-have gap (also the first `minor` severity on any fixture). Because a fixture is a mock and can only disagree quietly, the format is unit-tested directly in `packages/web/src/constants/skillCount.test.ts` (6 cases, `npm run test`), including assertions that it never emits a fraction or a reserved scale word.
- **No wire values change.** Presentation only; `strongMatches` / `partialMatches` / `gaps` and their `isRequired` flags are untouched.
- Specified in `docs/design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md` → "Match and Gap Section Counts". The stale `(5)` / `(2)` counts in the `COMPONENT_SPECS.md` Stage 3 wireframe are flagged there rather than redrawn, since that wireframe carries other `‹deferred›` divergences. Per-row disclosure remains asymmetric — partial-match rows say nothing, and on strong-match rows the _absence_ of a `Required` badge is what means nice-to-have — recorded as known residue.

### Fixed — The fit summary no longer restates the verdict, and the two middle rungs now order themselves (2026-08-26)

`strong_fit`'s summary opened **"Strong match — you meet 5 of 6 required skills."** and rendered three lines below a "Strong fit" label and three lines above a "✅ Strong Matches (N)" heading. That is one word carrying two meanings on one screen — the WIC-1288 defect class — except as a noun rather than an adjective: the summary's "match" was a whole-application verdict, the heading's is one skill's `matchType`. The two also count differently — the summary counts required strong **and** partial matches, the heading counts every strong match **including nice-to-haves** — so "you meet 5 of 6" could sit directly above "Strong Matches (7)". They agree only in the e2e fixture (5 strong, 0 partial, all required), which is what kept it invisible until the WIC-1297 copy review of PR #110 (WIC-1301).

- **The summary never restates the verdict** — the fit level label is the only place it is worded. `strong_fit` now opens with the same clause as every other rung: "You match N of M required skills." The rule this establishes: **the verdict axis owns "fit"; the match-classification axis owns "match"**, which is why "Strong fit" beside "Strong matches" is fine and "Strong match" beside it was not. With the prefix gone, the two lines no longer claim to be the same quantity, and the summary's "required skills" qualifier does the disambiguating.
- **`moderate_fit` gains the interpretive clause it was missing** — "This role is within reach." It was the only rung with no second clause, which left the ladder's weakest joint (**Possible fit** vs **Stretch**, post-WIC-1288) to be ordered by two labels that do not reliably order themselves: "possible" is the weakest modality word in English, while "a stretch role" is idiomatically aspirational. "Within reach" and "a stretch" are the same distance metaphor at two settings, so they order each other. The ladder now reads _nothing to add / within reach / a stretch / not yet_.
- **A clause states the verdict's stance, never a fact about the data** — `strong_fit` admits one critical required gap (`matchPct >= 0.8 && criticalGaps <= 1`), so the wording originally proposed on the card, _"Your profile covers the core requirements,"_ would have rendered immediately above " Gap in AWS." The top rung takes no clause at all instead: clauses are caveats, and the best case has none.
- **`computeSummary` is exported and unit-tested** (`packages/api/test/job-fit.service.test.ts`, 10 cases). Every surface that previously pinned these strings is a mocked fixture, so the generator and its fixtures could disagree indefinitely — which is precisely what happened. The e2e and route fixtures plus the `API_CONTRACTS.md` example response are also brought back into line with what the function actually emits.
- **No wire values change.** `summary` is a free-text response field; `recommendation` is untouched.
- Specified in `docs/design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md` → "Fit Level Summary", which also closes the open question left by WIC-1288's "The ladder is not ordinal in its words".
- **Docs corrected at the three places that disagreed or stayed silent** — `docs/design/COMPONENT_SPECS.md` said `0-100` and now says `0-1`, citing API_CONTRACTS as the source of record for the unit; `docs/architecture/DATA_MODEL.md` declared `responseRate` with no unit at all, directly above a code sample that computes a ratio; and API_CONTRACTS itself declared the field **twice** — `:557` carried the unit, `:722` did not, in the very document nominated as source of record. A sweep now confirms every `responseRate` declaration in `docs/` and `packages/` states its unit.

### Fixed — Gap severity now renders from one tokenised colour scale, not three disagreeing ones (2026-08-25)

The same `GapSeverity` value (`critical` / `moderate` / `minor`) was drawn by **three different colour ramps**, two of them on the same element. On a `JobFitAnalysis` gap card, `minor` was yellow by border and **green** by emoji; `moderate` was orange by border and yellow by emoji — so a user reading the border and a user reading the emoji got different severities off one card. `GapMitigationPanel` disagreed again, calling `minor` yellow, which is what `JobFitAnalysis` called `moderate`: the middle and low steps were effectively swapped between the two screens. Both sites now read the single `GAP_SEVERITY` map, so they cannot drift apart again (WIC-1146, implementing the scale decided in PR #96 / `docs/design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md` "Gap Severity Scale").

- **One shared source of truth** — `packages/web/src/constants/gapSeverity.ts` (new; this also establishes `constants/` as the home for shared non-component modules). It carries `label` plus the three token roles: `surface` tints the card, `mark` draws the left border and meets 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11), `text` colours the severity word and meets 4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3). The previous borders were raw palette values (`red-500` / `orange-500` / `yellow-500`), two of which missed the 3:1 non-text bar.
- **`minor` is amber, never green and not yellow (visible change)** — green reads as "resolved", and every gap is a shortfall; `yellow-500` is only 1.92:1 on white, and `yellow-700` collapses against `moderate` under deuteranopia (1.01:1). Amber restores what ordering this hue range permits.
- **The severity emoji are deleted, not replaced (visible change)** — 🔴/🟡/🟢 in `JobFitAnalysis` and 🔴/🟠/🟡 in `GapMitigationPanel`. They were the second, contradicting signal, and emoji cannot be tokenised at all: the platform font owns their hue, which is how the two components diverged in the first place. They are not swapped for a swatch or dot — a red→orange→amber ramp is not distinguishable under colour-vision deficiency (worst case 1.41:1 across the three dichromacies), so **the text label is the mandatory carrier of severity** (WCAG 1.4.1) and now does that work alone at both sites. In `GapMitigationPanel` the label takes the emoji's place as the row's visual anchor and keeps its badge caps from the Overline change below.
- **TC-6 un-skipped** — `job-fit-analysis.spec.ts`'s severity-styling test was skipped as flaky with the note "gap severity styling may vary". The variance was the bug itself; with one map the classes are deterministic. It now also asserts that no severity emoji survive.
- The `isAddressed` greyed-out treatment in `GapMitigationPanel` still overrides the severity surface, unchanged.

### Fixed — one TypeScript compiler over the repo, and `packages/web`'s strictness no longer depends on which command you typed (2026-08-30)

`typescript` resolved to two different versions in one tree: `node_modules/typescript` at **5.9.3** and `packages/web/node_modules/typescript` at **6.0.3**. Which one ran was decided by cwd, not by config — a root script (`npm run typecheck`) got 5.9.3, while `packages/web`'s own `build` (`tsc -b && vite build`, cwd `packages/web`) got 6.0.3. Neither `tsconfig.app.json` nor `tsconfig.node.json` declared `strict`, and TypeScript 6 defaults `strict` on where 5.9 leaves it off, so the strictness of every file in `packages/web` was a property of the invocation. All three `typescript` ranges are now `~6.0.2` and `strict` is stated explicitly in both web tsconfigs (WIC-1744, split out of WIC-1674 at the Code Reviewer's request on PR #232).

- **The split was not a lockfile accident, so it could not be fixed in the lockfile.** `packages/web` declared `~6.0.2` and `packages/api` declared `^5.4.5`; npm hoists one and nests the other, and `npm ci` at `9342655` reproduces the two copies from scratch. Nobody had ever chosen 5.9.3 — it was the hoisted resolution of the API's caret range, which also means the compiler behind the root `typecheck` script would have changed silently the next time that range was touched. The root `package.json` now declares `typescript` itself, so the binary a root script resolves is a stated fact rather than a hoisting outcome.
- **The divergence is reproduced against the real tree, not an isolated sample.** With the tsconfigs untouched at `9342655`, one file containing `export function f(x) { return x; }` and a `string | null` deref makes `tsc -p packages/web/tsconfig.app.json` exit **0** under 5.9.3 and **2** under 6.0.3 (`TS7006`, `TS18047`). After this change both `npm run typecheck` and `packages/web`'s `tsc -b --force` report that identical pair of diagnostics and both exit 2; on a clean tree both exit 0. That is the acceptance criterion, checked in both directions — a parity claim measured only on a green tree would pass with the type checker switched off entirely.
- **Declaring `strict: true` was a zero-diagnostic change, which is the evidence that aligning up was safe.** `packages/web` was already strict-clean: 0 errors under both compilers before and after, on `tsconfig.app.json` and `tsconfig.node.json` alike. It had been held to `strict` all along by CI running `npm run build` — the strict leg — so the alignment ratifies the standard the merged code already met instead of imposing a new one. Aligning *down* to 5.9.3 was rejected for the same reason: with the code already clean at 6.0.3 there was nothing to gain, and it would have re-weakened the only leg that gates a PR.
- **The API bump (`^5.4.5` → `~6.0.2`) is exercised, not assumed.** `packages/api` had `strict: true` already and carried no local compiler, so it had always run 5.9.3. Under 6.0.3 its real emitting `build` exits 0, and so do `npm run build:web` and `npm run lint` — the last of which matters because `typescript-eslint@8.58.2` bounds its peer at `>=4.8.4 <6.1.0`, and every `@typescript-eslint/*` package in the tree carries that same range. 6.0.3 is inside it; a 6.1 bump would not be.
- **`tsc --showConfig` cannot audit this and should not be used to.** It echoes only options the config file sets, so it reported `strict: undefined` under *both* compilers while they disagreed about the answer. The inherited default is invisible to the tool most likely to be reached for, which is the argument for writing the flag out rather than a matter of taste.
- **PR #232 merged first, so its section is reconciled here rather than replaced.** #232 landed on 2026-09-02 describing the divergence in the present tense, which this change falsifies in part. Rather than delete it, `CLAUDE.md` now separates its two causes: the two-compiler cause is closed by the pin, while the **cold-vs-warm `tsBuildInfoFile` cause it documents is untouched and still live**, so its cache-clearing reproduction recipe stays. The `dom-accessibility-api` guidance survives intact, with its one clause about the non-strict 5.9.3 root moved into the past tense — under one strict compiler `npm run typecheck` reports that `TS7016` too, which is the concrete payoff of the pin. The earlier note on #232 asking for it to be cut down is withdrawn.

### Security — Resume-variant and interview-prep reads are scoped to the caller on every table they touch (2026-08-27)

`resume-variant.service.ts` and `interviewPrep.service.ts` scoped reads of their _own_ tables to the caller and then read `resumes`, `tech_stack_tags` and `applications` on a caller-supplied id with **no owner term at all**. Separately, every owner-bearing predicate in both services was `userId ? and(idTerm, ownerTerm) : idTerm`, so a caller without a `sub` claim read the whole table. Both are closed (WIC-1601, filed out of the PR #203 / WIC-1537 review).

- **Seven reads gained an owner term.** `generateResumeVariant` accepted another user's `baseResumeId` and `selectedTechTags` — existence oracles over `resumes` and `tech_stack_tags` — and then persisted the foreign `baseResumeId`, which `getResumeVariant` read back out as that user's `fileName`. `generateInterviewPrep` read another user's `applications` row and put its `jobTitle`/`company` into the LLM prompt and into the generated prep; its uniqueness probe answered `409` with a **foreign** prep id in `details.existingPrepId`. `getInterviewPrep` and `exportInterviewPrep` re-read `applications` off the prep's stored `applicationId`, so the export filename could carry another user's company name. Fixing the write path does not clean the rows it already wrote, so the reads carry the predicate too and a foreign reference now degrades to absent.
- **The absent-caller branch fails closed.** A shared `ownerScope(table, userId)` returns `isNull(table.userId)` instead of `undefined`, so "anonymous" means _the rows nobody owns_, not _every row_ — the fail-open idiom WIC-1482 recorded on `fetchStarEntries` and WIC-1500 found reachable through a `sub`-less JWT. `resume_variants`, `interview_preps`, `resumes` and `applications` all have a nullable `user_id` and insert `userId ?? null`, so the ADR-003 local-dev bypass is unchanged. `tech_stack_tags.user_id` is `NOT NULL` since migration `0017`, so an anonymous caller there reaches the empty set — deliberate, and pinned by a test that says so.
- **RLS is not the backstop.** The policies in `0002_rls_current_schema.sql` are `TO authenticated USING (auth.uid() = user_id)`, but the Worker connects over a raw `postgres://` string and never sets a JWT claim, so `auth.uid()` is NULL and they never apply. The predicate has to be in the query.
- **Accepted against a 22-cell mutation matrix**, each cell run alone and each landing on exactly the kill count predicted before the run, with three negative controls (predicates that carry no owner term, guarded upstream) staying green. The seven previously-unscoped reads were run red against the unfixed tree first, each naming the value it leaked. Documented in full in `packages/api/test/resume-variant-interview-prep.tenancy.test.ts`.
- The `quantified_bullets` half of the original report is **not** in this change — all seven of those sites are fixed on the WIC-1449 branch (PR #153), which was not in this branch's base when the card was written.
- **`generateInterviewPrep` is a hijack, not only a disclosure (WIC-1549).** The unscoped read above also fell through to an `INSERT`, and `interview_preps.application_id` is **UNIQUE** — so the first stranger to reach it consumed the only prep slot the application will ever have and locked the owner out behind a permanent `409`. **What this change closes, and what it does not:** new hijacks are blocked — no stranger can reach the insert any more. Applications that *already* carry a foreign prep are not repaired, and their owners remain locked out, now behind an unhandled `23505` UNIQUE violation (a 500, no `statusCode`) rather than the clean `APPLICATION_ALREADY_HAS_PREP` 409, because the now-scoped uniqueness probe no longer matches the foreign row. Triaging that population by 409 will find none of it. Mapping the error and backfilling those rows is deliberately out of scope here and tracked as WIC-1622. Pinned on PGlite rather than a stub, because the UNIQUE violation is the severity and only a real engine raises it: each refusal asserts the `db.insert` spy never fired, the table is really empty, and the foreign company never reached the model, against a positive control that shows all three inverted. Five further cells, each at its predicted kill count; `getInterviewPrep`'s and `exportInterviewPrep`'s `applications` reads are **negative controls that stay green**, since they take their id from an already-owner-scoped `prep`. See `packages/api/test/interview-prep.generate.tenancy.test.ts`.
- **The anonymous positive control now pins the fail-closed posture instead of success.** Merging `main` in brought WIC-1485/1449's owner scope onto this service's `quantified_bullets` read, and that column is `.notNull()` since `0017_enforce_userid_not_null.sql` — so an absent caller's `IS NULL` predicate matches no rows by construction, the catalog reads empty, and `CATALOG_EMPTY` is raised before the insert. The old "succeeds for an absent caller" expectation was written against the pre-fix global read and is now unsatisfiable by design, not by fixture; the service states the intent in as many words ("Failing closed is the intent"). Rewritten to assert the refusal *and* that the unowned application's UNIQUE slot is left unconsumed. Falsifiability is unaffected — the owner positive control above still proves the function inserts under some circumstances — and the new assertion was mutation-checked: dropping the owner scope from the read kills exactly this test, 7 of 7 cases still executing.

### Job Fit Analysis — overall fit and gap severity de-shouted (2026-08-19)

The two remaining ALL-CAPS renders in `JobFitAnalysis` were mid-sentence caps at 20px and 14px, not Overline badges (Overline is 10px/600), so both are now sentence case. Each enum renders through a typed label map instead of `.toUpperCase().replace('_', ' ')`, so an added `Recommendation` or `GapSeverity` member is a compile error rather than a raw enum key on screen. The overall fit result is also promoted out of its sentence into a label-over-value pair built from existing type-scale steps — it is the headline answer of the screen and was previously carried only by shouting. Visible change; no logic change (WIC-1122, correcting the classification made in WIC-1069).

### Security — catalog merge endpoints are scoped to the calling user (2026-08-26)

The three catalog merge services took the caller's user id and ignored it — the parameter was named `_userId` and never referenced, so every lookup and every write inside them was keyed on row id alone. An authenticated user who knew or guessed a ULID could operate on another user's catalog: `POST /api/catalog/companies/merge` folded another user's companies into a target and soft-deleted the sources, and the two tag merge routes **hard-deleted** each source row with no recovery path. The routes were never at fault; they threaded `c.get('userId')` through correctly (WIC-1365, surfaced reviewing PR #124).

- **Both reads and both writes now carry the tenancy predicate.** Scoping only the read would still leave the destructive half exploitable, because the follow-up `UPDATE`/`DELETE` matched on id alone — a source row the scoped read excluded would have been deleted anyway. The tag deletes now iterate the rows the scoped read returned rather than the caller's raw id list.
- **Single-user/local mode is unchanged.** The predicate is conditional on `userId` being present, matching `resolveDiffItem` and the `list*` functions in the same file, so with `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` unset (`userId` null) the emitted SQL is byte-for-byte what it was before. Three tests pin that explicitly.
- **A row the caller does not own reports `NotFoundError`, not 403** — consistent with `resolveDiffItem`, and it avoids confirming that the id exists.
- **Tests assert the rendered SQL, not the call count.** The service tests serialise the Drizzle where-clause through `PgDialect` and assert on the predicate, so deleting the `eq(table.userId, userId)` term fails them; reverting the fix fails 5 of them. The route tests gained an authenticated block that signs an HS256 JWT and pins the caller's `sub` reaching each of the three services — the pre-existing cases assert `undefined` there, which was right for an unauthenticated harness but read as "the user id is not part of the merge contract".

### Docs — the four onboarding endpoints are specified, including the scoped AC-10 bypass (2026-08-26)

`API_CONTRACTS.md` documented no onboarding endpoint at all — `grep -n onboarding` returned nothing, and no file under `docs/` mentioned `should-show`. Four routes had shipped unspecified, and WIC-1359 had just given one of them semantics that read as arbitrary without their rationale attached. Docs only; no source change (WIC-1367, filed by Backend from WIC-1359).

- **`should-show` is documented as the sole authority on visibility, in the imperative.** The contract now says plainly that clients must not derive visibility from the status row, and says why: `GET /status` auto-creates a `welcome` row, so testing `completedAt`/`currentStep` shows onboarding to every established user. That is the WIC-1359 defect restated as a rule, placed where the next implementer reads before writing rather than in a postmortem they will not open.
- **The AC-10 bypass is documented as scoped in time, with the reasoning that makes it stick.** A three-row decision table gives the shipped precedence — completed, then engaged, then the pristine/no-row case — and names `started_at` as the discriminator on the engaged branch, with the argument for it: the resume-upload step _produces_ a resume, so an unbounded history check would eject a new user from the flow at the moment its own step succeeded, while treating engagement as unconditional consent would show onboarding forever to an established user who pressed "Skip for now" once. The table also records why the bound is applied on the engaged branch only and deliberately not on the pristine one. Recording the rule without the argument would invite either "simplification" back.
- **`GET /status`'s write side effect is called out as a warning, not a footnote.** A doc that presents it as a plain read is what makes the auto-initialization easy to miss, and the auto-created row is the mechanism behind the whole blast radius.
- **Two spec-drift items recorded so they are not re-derived as defects** — the step enum ships five values, not the four in the accepted WIC-238 spec (`personal_info` arrived in migration `0015` afterwards), and there is no `/onboarding` page route despite AC-1 naming one (the flow is a global `<OnboardingModal />` in `App.tsx`).
- **Three behaviours were measured rather than read off the source**, since each is the kind of thing a doc gets wrong by inference: a malformed JSON body on `/progress` returns `500 INTERNAL_ERROR` rather than `400` (the body is parsed before Zod sees it, so the `SyntaxError` misses the `AppError` handler), an empty `{}` body is a valid version-bumping no-op, and unknown keys are stripped rather than rejected. The `500` is documented as a known rough edge, not as a guarantee.
- **The `401`-under-local-bypass case is documented**, because it is the one place these routes diverge from the rest of the API: with `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` both unset the middleware passes requests through with `userId = null`, and onboarding refuses rather than operating on an anonymous user — so unlike most endpoints these are unusable in single-user local mode without a token.
- **`ONBOARDING_FLOW.md` corrected where it contradicted the shipped API.** Its endpoint sketch advertised a `POST /onboarding/dismiss` route that does not exist and request bodies that were never built, and its trigger conditions stated the blanket "zero resumes and zero applications" rule that WIC-1359 disproved — leaving the design doc as a live source of exactly the misreading this change exists to prevent. Both now defer to the API contract, and the non-existent dismissed state is named as such.

### Security — App-host transport hardening (2026-08-19)

QA's WIC-1003 prod regression pass found `app.careerpin.app` — the authenticated surface, carrying Supabase session tokens, resume uploads and PII — serving the app shell over plaintext HTTP with a `200` and sending **no** security headers at all, while the marketing apex and `www` both `301` to HTTPS. Root cause: the app host is a Workers custom domain, so the zone-level HTTPS redirect that covers apex/www does not reach it, and neither the Worker nor the static-asset router was emitting hardening headers (WIC-1011).

- **Cleartext requests are redirected** — `httpsRedirect()` (`packages/api/src/middleware/security.ts`) turns away any request that arrived over HTTP before a handler runs: `301` for `GET`/`HEAD`, `308` for methods with a body so the retry keeps its method and payload. The client scheme is read from Cloudflare's `cf-visitor` — the only authoritative source at the edge — then the request URL. `x-forwarded-proto` is client-settable unless a trusted proxy rewrites it, so it is honoured only when `TRUST_PROXY_PROTO` is set; otherwise a spoofed `x-forwarded-proto: https` on a cleartext request still gets redirected. Private hosts are exempt — loopback, RFC1918/link-local literals, `*.local`/`*.internal`-style suffixes and dotless container names — so `npm run dev:api` / `wrangler dev` / Vitest, LAN and mobile testing, and container-network access by service name all stay on plain HTTP rather than being upgraded to a `:443` nothing listens on.
- **Security headers on every response** — `securityHeaders()` attaches `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` and `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`, without clobbering a value a handler already set. Responses that came out of `fetch()` — notably the `ASSETS` binding serving the SPA shell — have immutable headers, so the middleware rebuilds them rather than dropping the hardening. HSTS `preload` is deliberately withheld until the cleartext `301` is confirmed live, since preloading is not reversible on a useful timescale. A full CSP beyond `frame-ancestors` awaits an audit of the Supabase/PostHog/R2 origins the SPA talks to.
- **Static assets carry the same headers** — the asset router answers `/`, `/assets/*` and `/favicon.svg` _before_ the Worker runs, so those responses can only be hardened at the edge. `packages/web/public/_headers` (copied verbatim into `packages/web/dist/`, the `assets.directory`) declares the same five headers.
- **Fingerprinted assets are now immutable** — Vite content-hashes everything under `/assets/`, but the Cloudflare default `public, max-age=0, must-revalidate` cost a revalidation round-trip per asset per page load. Those are now `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`; `index.html` is explicitly held at `must-revalidate` so clients cannot pin to a stale build and request asset hashes that no longer exist.
- **The first-contact gap was closed at the zone, not in code** — the Worker-side redirect only covers paths the Worker actually sees (`/api/*`, `/health`, SPA deep links); `/` and `/assets/*` are answered by the static-asset router before the Worker runs, so no code change could reach them. HSTS does not paper over this: per RFC 6797 §8.1 a browser **must ignore** an HSTS header received over plain HTTP, so the `_headers` HSTS on a cleartext `/` pins nothing — the pin only lands once a client completes an HTTPS response. The actual fix was the zone-level `Always Use HTTPS` setting on the `careerpin.app` zone, enabled 2026-08-19 under WIC-1014 and verified live: `curl -sI http://app.careerpin.app/` → `301` → `https://app.careerpin.app/`, with apex and `www` unchanged. HSTS `preload` remains deliberately withheld: it is now eligible (the `301` is confirmed), but submitting the domain is a separate, hard-to-reverse decision tracked apart from this change.
- **HSTS and `nosniff` also ship from the zone, ahead of this deploy** — for the same reason the redirect had to: the asset router answers `/` before the Worker runs, and `_headers` only takes effect on a deploy. The `careerpin.app` zone `security_header` setting was enabled 2026-08-19 (WIC-1011) with `max-age=31536000`, `includeSubDomains`, `nosniff`, and `preload` **off** — byte-identical to the values in `SECURITY_HEADERS` and `_headers`, so nothing drifts when this branch lands, and `securityHeaders()` only sets a header it does not already see. Verified live on all three hosts: `strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` and `x-content-type-options: nosniff` on `app`, apex and `www`. `includeSubDomains` is safe here because every record in the zone is Cloudflare-proxied (including a proxied `*.careerpin.app` wildcard) with `Always Use HTTPS` on, so there is no plaintext-only host to strand. The remaining three headers (`X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Content-Security-Policy`) and the immutable `/assets/*` `Cache-Control` are **not** reachable from the zone — the production API token is authorised for zone settings but not for the response-header transform ruleset (`request is not authorized`) — so those still ship only with this deploy.

### Fixed — Onboarding refused valid resumes, and could record a step as both done and skipped (2026-08-26)

Three conformance defects in the onboarding **client**, traced against the accepted WIC-238 criteria and against the API the client talks to (D-7, D-5, D-9). All three were invisible to the API suite: every one of them lived in `packages/web`, which had no onboarding coverage at all, so `packages/api` stayed green through the lot. That absence is the reason this cluster existed, so the fix ships with the tests (WIC-1382).

- **A 7 MB PDF is no longer refused (D-7, the user-visible one)** — `ResumeUploadZone` capped uploads at 5 MB while the API accepts 10 MB (`MAX_FILE_SIZE`, `packages/api/src/routes/resumes.ts`) and accepted AC-3/AC-4 put the boundary at 10 MB, and the onboarding call site passed no override. A resume the spec calls valid and the server would have taken was rejected at the highest-drop-off moment in the product, with no way around it. The limit now lives in one place (`packages/web/src/constants/upload.ts`); both the error message and the format hint derive from it, so they cannot disagree with the check.
- **The two limits can no longer drift apart, which was the actual root cause** — `upload.drift.test.ts` pulls the API route in as text via Vite's `?raw` and fails if its `MAX_FILE_SIZE` stops matching the client constant. A shared workspace package was considered and rejected: `packages/api` builds with `tsc` under `rootDir: ./src`, so a shared TS module would have forced a build-order change to the deploy workflow. The guard buys the same protection for none of that risk. It fails **loudly** rather than vacuously if the API constant is renamed or moved — verified by doing exactly that.
- **A step is now done, or skipped, or neither — never both (D-5)** — `handleResumeUploadSuccess` cleared its counterpart flag but `handlePersonalInfoSubmit`, `handleSkipPersonalInfo` and `handleSkipResume` did not. Steps 2 and 3 both render a Back button, so *skip Personal Info → Next → Back → submit* left `personalInfoStepCompleted` and `personalInfoStepSkipped` both true, and the resume step had the same hole in reverse. The six booleans exist precisely to tell *done* from *skipped* from *not yet reached*; once both can be true the model collapses to a single "touched" bit and **Skip Rate by Step** — a WIC-238 success metric — stops being countable.
- **Enforced server-side as well, so a stale client cannot reintroduce it** — `updateOnboardingProgress` spread the patch verbatim; it now clears the counterpart whenever either member of a pair is set `true`, covering every caller rather than just the one that was fixed. A single patch naming both flags as `true` is contradictory on its face and is now a `400` from `progressSchema`, not a silent precedence rule the caller never asked for. A compile-time guard fails the build if a future step adds a flag pair and forgets to register it — and in the reverse direction, if a pair is dropped from the registry while its flags survive on the interface.
- **Removed a second, staler source of truth for the current step (D-9)** — an effect wrote `onboarding_progress` to `localStorage` on every step change and **nothing ever read it back**; resumption is driven entirely by the server record via `STEP_TO_NUMBER[status.currentStep]`. Harmless as it stood, but it read like a resume mechanism, and the next reader to wire it up believing that would have given the app two disagreeing answers to which step the user is on. Deleted rather than adopted by accident: client-side resumption, if it is ever wanted, has to be reconciled against the server record deliberately.
- **Coverage** — 11 web tests (`OnboardingModal.test.tsx`, `upload.drift.test.ts`) and 14 API tests (`onboarding-step-flags.test.ts`), including the exact skip → back → submit path from the report and its resume-step mirror. Each guard was checked against a deliberately reverted fix and each one fails when the defect is restored, so none of them is decorative.

### Docs — COMPONENT_SPECS wireframe casing is now marked per line instead of derived (2026-08-26)

The casing note at the top of `docs/design/COMPONENT_SPECS.md` asked readers to sort a shouted wireframe line into "heading" (a bug) or "badge" (intentional). An ASCII wireframe renders both as the same glyphs, so every reader re-derived the split by hand and some derived it wrong — producing four tickets that each found the same defect further down the same file (WIC-1069 → WIC-1184 → WIC-1187 → WIC-1195). Docs only; no source or rendered output changes (WIC-1195).

- **Intent is now marked on the line, not inferred** — intentional-caps lines carry a trailing `‹overline›`, non-UI-string lines (placeholders, example content, acronyms, annotations) carry `‹sample›`, and lines whose fix is owned by another ticket carry `‹deferred›`, with an owner table in the note. The rule collapses to one sentence with no judgement in it: **a caps label with no marker is a defect.** 53 wireframe rows changed in all — 25 de-shouted, 28 marked. Markers sit outside the closing box border, so no wireframe alignment changed: every changed row is identical to its predecessor modulo case and the appended marker, and an East-Asian-width-aware measure reports 0 width drift across all 53.
- **25 wireframe lines de-shouted** to the strings their components actually ship — `QuestionsList` (5), `GapMitigationPanel` (3), and 17 unbuilt-spec headings that take sentence case by default. The triage that drove this had missed three lines (`TASK` in both STAR blocks, and `STORY:`); the sweep is now mechanical and exhaustive rather than hand-enumerated, which is what let the earlier passes leave residue.
- **The note's over-strong clause is corrected** — it previously said a shouted heading must always be de-shouted. A heading uppercased by a CSS `uppercase` class is _correct_: the caps never reach the accessibility tree, so "fixing" it in the source string would be the mirror-image defect. `ResumeVariantDetail` is the model case and is now marked as such.
- **Colon-terminated labels get their own clause** — a source string ending in `:` is an inline field label introducing the content beneath it, never an Overline, so it is de-shouted with no `uppercase` class (`Key phrases:`, `Redirect to:` — WIC-1205). The test reads off the source string, not the wireframe: `🔴 CRITICAL:` draws a separator colon the source does not contain. This also makes the convention self-checking — `‹overline›` on a colon-terminated label is a contradiction rather than merely a lookup miss.
- **The convention is machine-checkable, not just written down** — `docs/design/wireframe-casing-audit.py` walks every fenced wireframe block and exits non-zero on any unmarked caps label. It is what makes the note self-terminating: the next shouted line fails a check instead of waiting to become ticket number five. Running it also caught a real defect in this change's own first draft, which excluded "runs in which no word reaches four letters" as acronyms — `STAR` and `DOCX` are four letters, so that heuristic demanded markers on ~20 acronym lines while `TASK`, a genuine label, is also four. The rule is now **positional**: a label opens its box row and is followed by nothing but trailing space, a colon, or a right-aligned badge; caps inside a sentence are acronyms. The script documents its own limit — it checks row-leading labels only, so a mid-row run such as `Overall Fit: MODERATE FIT` is still the reader's job.
- **Nothing is left deferred to an open ticket** — the two `GapMitigationPanel` lines (`KEY PHRASES:` / `REDIRECT TO:`) carried `‹deferred›` pointing at WIC-1205 while its source fix was unmerged; WIC-1205 now lands the source fix and de-shouts these wireframe rows in the same change, so the markers and their owner-table row are gone. The QuickReferenceExport wireframes that earlier drafts of this entry deferred to PR #100 / PR #102 are likewise no longer deferred: those PRs and PR #98 have all merged, so those lines already match what the component ships. The only rows still marked `‹deferred›` point at genuinely unbuilt components (StoryEditor) or another live ticket (§13 `MODERATE FIT`).

### Documentation — The four remaining UC-5 report endpoints are now specified (2026-08-25)

`API_CONTRACTS.md` had no `Reports (UC-5)` section until the entry below added one, and that entry deliberately specified only `GET /api/reports/by-fit-tier` — the one endpoint with a cross-use-case contract to state. The other four shipped with UC-5 in April 2026 and had never been specified anywhere: `GET /api/reports/pipeline`, `/needs-action`, `/stale` and `/closed-loop` are now documented from the Zod query schemas in `routes/reports.ts` and the response interfaces in `types/index.ts` (WIC-1307). No behaviour changed — this records what the endpoints already do.

Three properties were undocumented and are not guessable from the response shape:

- **Summaries on the paginated reports describe the page, not the result set.** `needs-action`, `stale` and `closed-loop` compute every `summary` field — `total` included — from the current page, after `limit` is applied. `summary.total` is the length of `applications`, never a grand total, and the averages and breakdowns are page-local. A client reading `summary.total` as a result-set count under-reports by a factor of however many pages there are.
- **`GET /api/reports/stale` defaults to `applied,phone_screen`, not to all statuses.** Those are the two states where the ball is in the employer's court. Callers expecting every active application to be eligible for staleness must pass `status` explicitly.
- **`closed-loop`'s `rejectionsByStage` need not account for every rejection.** It buckets by `previousStatus`, so rejections whose history is too short to have one count toward `summary.rejections` while appearing in no bucket, and `percentage` is a share of `rejections` rather than of `total`. The percentages sum to 100 only when every rejection has a known previous stage.

Also recorded: `pipeline` and `by-fit-tier` are unpaginated and accept neither `limit` nor `cursor`; `limit` above 100 is a `400` rather than a clamp; `pipeline`'s application objects carry no `status` field because the group supplies it; and `closed-loop`'s `period` filters on `updatedAt` rather than the computed `closedAt`, so editing a closed application keeps it inside a narrow window.

The shared section also now carries the **malformed-cursor `400`** that WIC-1308 shipped (see the entry above): a `cursor` the server did not issue is a `VALIDATION_ERROR` on `needs-action`, `stale` and `closed-loop`, with **no `details`** — the second `VALIDATION_ERROR` shape on these endpoints, and the Zod block is cross-referenced so a reader does not assume every report `400` carries `details`. That block claimed the route schemas were "the authority on accepted values", which `cursor` is the one exception to — it is declared as a plain optional string and judged only when it is decoded in `reports.service.ts` — so the claim now carves it out rather than being contradicted three lines later (WIC-1316). An absent or empty `cursor` is still the first page. Two encoding leaks were closed on `main` by `172802b` (#120), not here (WIC-1311): the pagination table and the catalog-diffs table had both published the cursor as a "base64url-encoded offset" while the prose two lines below called the encoding an implementation detail — publishing the recipe is an invitation to hand-craft exactly the cursor now being rejected. This branch's `109b18c` made the same edit independently about twenty minutes later, so merging `main` in absorbed the duplicate and this change's net diff carries none of it. Both rows now say what the cursor _is_ (opaque, server-issued) rather than how it is built.

### Fixed — Every paginated endpoint now rejects a malformed cursor, from one shared decoder (2026-08-25)

WIC-1308 fixed the unguarded base64url cursor decode in `reports.service.ts`. The identical decode was inlined, unguarded, at **nine more call sites across four services** — `catalog` (six), `application`, `cover-letter`, `resume-variant` — none of which had even the unreachable `try`/`catch` the reports version started with. Both failure modes carried over verbatim (WIC-1312).

- **Encoder and decoder now live together**, in `packages/api/src/lib/pagination.ts`. `encodeCursor` was copy-pasted at all twelve sites too; that every site could _mint_ a cursor while only the reports trio could _reject_ one is precisely how the guard came to be missing in nine places. The reports service now imports both rather than owning them.
- **Reject, not fall back — at all twelve sites, including the catalog ones.** `API_CONTRACTS.md:713` publishes the catalog cursor's encoding ("base64url-encoded offset") rather than calling it opaque, which raised the question of whether a hand-crafted catalog cursor is supported. It does not change the answer: a hand-crafted cursor that genuinely _is_ a base64url non-negative offset still works, so the only requests this turns into a `400` are ones no correct client can send.
- **`GET /api/applications` is the odd one out and was checked separately**, per the ticket. Its parameter is `page`, not `cursor` — but `nextPage` is minted the same way (`Buffer.from(String(offset + limit))`), it is documented as coming "from a previous response", and no client constructs one, so the same `400` applies. Its `catch` was doubly dead: unreachable _and_ the comment above it ("start from beginning") described a fallback that would not have happened anyway. The error message names `page`/`nextPage` rather than `cursor`/`nextCursor`, so it points at something the caller can find in their own request.
- **The guard is verified to be wired in at each site, not merely to exist.** `packages/api/test/pagination.test.ts` drives all twelve real service functions with a malformed cursor and a negative one against a database handle that throws on any access — so a site that skips the guard is caught by reaching the query builder, which is the actual defect. Confirmed by mutation: restoring the inline decode at `catalog.listCompanies` and `application.listApplications` fails exactly their four cases, each reporting `db.select was reached with a malformed cursor`. The `parseCursor` unit cases move here from `reports.service.test.ts` alongside them. API suite: 411 passing.
- **The coverage table is now counted rather than trusted (WIC-1335).** Its first draft listed only the nine sites this change converted and omitted the three in `reports.service.ts` — the ones WIC-1308 was about — so its own claim that "reverting any single site fails its case here" was false for a quarter of the codebase. Measured on review: reinstating the exact pre-WIC-1308 decode in `getNeedsActionReport` left the whole suite green. The three rows are added, and a companion case now compares `parseCursor` call sites found in `src/services/*.ts` against the table **per service**, so neither a new paginated endpoint nor a swapped row can shrink the claim silently. Confirmed by mutation in both directions: each reports site now fails its own two cases, and dropping a row — or trading one service's row for another's, leaving the total unchanged — fails the counter.
- **The error message no longer infers the response field from the request parameter.** It built the field name as `next${param === 'page' ? 'Page' : 'Cursor'}`, so a future endpoint spelling its parameter anything else would have been told to pass back a `nextCursor` its response does not contain. `parseCursor` now takes both names as one `{ param, responseField }` value (`CURSOR_NAMES`, `PAGE_NAMES`). The two messages that exist today are byte-identical to before — this closes a latent trap, it does not change the contract.
- **Documentation divergence found, not fixed here** — `API_CONTRACTS.md` documents the applications list parameter as `cursor` returning `nextCursor`; the implementation has always used `page`/`nextPage`. A client following the document sends `cursor=…`, which the Zod schema drops silently, so it receives page one forever with no error. Pre-existing and independent of this change; handed to the Technical Writer with the cursor-contract update.

### Fixed — The by-fit-tier page can no longer drop a whole tier without failing the build (2026-08-25)

`FIT_TIER_ORDER` on the API is guarded by `_FIT_TIER_ORDER_IS_EXHAUSTIVE`, so a new fit tier that nothing ranks is a compile error rather than a set of applications quietly missing from the report. The page rendering that report had no equivalent. `VERDICT_TIERS` in `ReportsByFitTier.tsx` was annotated `Extract<FitTier, 'strong_fit' | 'moderate_fit' | 'stretch' | 'low_fit'>` — a **filter**, not an exhaustiveness assertion. Removing a tier narrowed it and errored; **adding** one was simply not selected, silently. Found reviewing PR #111 (WIC-1310); no such member exists today, so nothing has shipped wrong.

- **The failure was reproduced before it was fixed.** Adding `'perfect_fit'` to `Recommendation` and giving it a label — the one-line change any developer would make, because `FIT_LEVEL_LABELS`' own `satisfies Record<NonNullable<Recommendation>, string>` is what breaks first — left `npx tsc -b packages/web --noEmit` at exit `0` with **no tile for the new tier**. The API would have returned it in `groups` and counted it in `summary.byTier`; the page renders a hard-listed array and would have dropped it.
- **The hard-listed four names are gone.** `VerdictTier` is now `Exclude<FitTier, 'unscored' | 'not_analyzed'>` — derived by exclusion, so a new `Recommendation` member joins it by construction instead of waiting to be added to a filter by hand. The two no-verdict states keep their own row above the tiles, and that decision is now written down where it is enforced rather than only in a comment.
- **The hazard is an explicit type annotation on `VERDICT_TIERS`, not the loss of `as const`.** The guard reads `typeof VERDICT_TIERS`, so it only sees the entry literals while that type is *inferred*. Measured four ways with `'perfect_fit'` added: `as const satisfies` catches it; **`satisfies` alone also catches it** — deleting `as const` breaks nothing; but a `ReadonlyArray<{ tier: VerdictTier; … }>` annotation widens every entry's `tier` to the whole union, makes `UntiledVerdictTier` vacuously `never`, and exits `0` — **even with `as const satisfies` still present**. `as const` only makes the array readonly; `satisfies` is what constrains the shape without replacing the inferred type. *(Corrected from the original bullet, which named `as const` as load-bearing and so pointed a maintainer at the wrong thing to preserve — WIC-1337.)*
- **That correction is enforced, not just written down.** An annotation is a plausible edit — a lint preference, a "be explicit" review note, an IDE quick-fix — and it disables the exhaustiveness check with a clean build and no other signal. `_VERDICT_TIERS_KEEPS_ENTRY_LITERALS` now fails compilation if any entry's `tier` is the whole `VerdictTier` union rather than one name, which is exactly what an annotation does to every entry at once. It names no tier literal, so reordering or renaming tiles leaves it alone. It tests the entry union by distribution rather than indexing entry `[0]`: `[0]` means "entry zero" only while the type is a *tuple*, so on an array it yields the union of all four entries and reads as widened — a guard that failed a sound tree. That false positive was caught in review and is measured below (WIC-1361).
- **Verified in ten directions, not one.** Unmodified tree: exit `0`, no false positive. Adding `'perfect_fit'` to `Recommendation` plus its label: fails naming `"perfect_fit"`, sole error. Deleting the `low_fit` tile: fails naming `"low_fit"` — the protection the old `Extract` did provide is retained. Giving `'unscored'` a tile: rejected at the constraint, which the filter form also missed. Annotating `VERDICT_TIERS` **with** `as const satisfies` intact: fails on the annotation guard (before this change, exit `0`). Annotating it **without** `satisfies`: same failure. Annotation **and** `'perfect_fit'` together: the annotation guard fires, so widening cannot mask an added tier — the two guards compose. Reordering the tiles: exit `0`. **Deleting `as const` while keeping `satisfies`: exit `0`** — and deleting it *with* `'perfect_fit'` added still fails naming `"perfect_fit"`, which is what makes the bullet above true rather than merely plausible. `packages/api/test/fit-tier-blurbs.test.ts` re-reads these entries out of the source by regex and still passes, so the cross-package blurb check is unaffected.

### Fixed — By-fit-tier tile blurbs no longer contradict the tier they label (2026-08-25)

Each tile on `GET /api/reports/by-fit-tier`'s page carried a one-line blurb describing its tier, and every blurb restated only the **match-percentage** arm of `computeRecommendation`. That function is an ordered four-way cascade over _three_ variables — match percentage, critical-gap count, and the seniority flag — so a tier fires far outside the percentage band its blurb claimed. Found reviewing PR #111 (WIC-1309); the tiles are `opacity-50` placeholders rendering `—` today because UC-3 analyses are not persisted, so nothing user-visible has shipped wrong yet.

- **Measured, not argued.** Exercising the real `computeRecommendation` over every reachable `(match %, critical gaps, seniority)` triple at `totalRequired = 20` — 574 cases, match percentage in half-steps because partial matches weigh 0.5 — the shipped blurbs were false for **81 of them (14.1%)**. The worst case: a 100% skill match with 3 critical gaps returns `moderate_fit`, so the tier would have been captioned **"50–79% of required skills"** — contradicting its own definition, and contradicting the **"You match 20 of 20 required skills"** the same user reads when they drill into the application. (The number on the tile itself is the count of applications in that tier, not a skill-match count; no skill-match count is rendered on the report page.) The independently-reported figure on a coarser 252-case grid was 32 (12.7%).
- **Blurbs are now necessary conditions of their tier, never sufficient ones.** A tile has no room to restate a cascade and does not need to; what it must never do is make a claim its own tier can violate. Each of the four now carries the gap and seniority conditions that can pull a tier down. Re-measured over the same grid: **0 violations.**
- **The invariant is enforced, not just fixed.** `packages/api/test/fit-tier-blurbs.test.ts` pairs each shipped string with a machine-readable predicate, checks it against the real scorer over the whole grid, and re-reads the strings **out of `ReportsByFitTier.tsx`** — cross-package on purpose, because the copy lives in `web`, the rule lives in `api`, and nothing else connected the two. Reword a blurb without revisiting its predicate and the API suite fails. A companion assertion pins that all four tiers are actually reached, so the check cannot pass vacuously. Confirmed by reversal: restoring the original blurbs fails it with 81 named counterexamples.
- **The source doc had the same defect and is corrected in the same change.** `docs/architecture/API_CONTRACTS.md`'s scoring bullets (pre-existing, and almost certainly where the blurbs were copied from) read as four exclusive percentage bands. They are an **ordered cascade**: the first rule that matches wins, so a tier's range is not bounded above by the tier before it. `strong_fit`'s ≤1-critical-gap condition was unstated, `moderate_fit` was documented as 50–79% when it fires up to 100%, `stretch` did not mention the >3-critical-gap route into it, and `low_fit` omitted that it also requires no seniority mismatch.
- **Wording settled in the same change (WIC-1318).** The engineer-written strings were true but read as spec lines. Reworded on one principle: **no tile spends more than two clauses, and the cascade is legible across the set rather than inside any one tile.** The gap ladder now reads off two tiles (`strong_fit` "at most one critical gap", `stretch` "more than three critical gaps", which leaves 2–3 for `moderate_fit`) and the seniority axis off two more (`moderate_fit` "with no seniority mismatch", `stretch` "or a seniority mismatch"), so `moderate_fit` sheds its third clause and `low_fit` its second without either losing something a reader needed.
